title: The open AI-native stack on Kubernetes: From open models to distributed inference and agents
raw_text:
Over the past decade, Kubernetes established itself as the standard for orchestrating microservices and containerized applications. Today, we're witnessing the next major architectural shift in distributed computing: AI workloads moving from isolated research prototypes into large-scale, multi-tenant production fleets . In this post, we'll walk through the open-source stack that powers this shift and show you the sample manifests that you can try on your own Kubernetes clusters. You can also join us at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 to see these projects in action through live demos and technical sessions. For modern engineering teams, production AI is rapidly moving beyond generic calls to closed, black-box APIs. Organizations are realizing that their long-term competitive advantage lies in domain specialization. Platform engineers, ML researchers, and AI builders want the autonomy to run high-performing open-weight models (such as the Gemma family). They want to adapt them to proprietary enterprise datasets by using reinforcement learning (RL) and serve them with predictable latency, high throughput, and maximum hardware efficiency. Whether it's scientific initiatives training domain models like DolphinGemma (an LLM helping scientists study how dolphins communicate) on acoustic data, legal platforms evaluating complex contracts, or engineering teams building autonomous coding agents, the objective is the same: achieving frontier-level task performance at a fraction of the serving cost and latency. Yet, scaling RL post-training, stateful distributed inference, and autonomous agent execution on traditional container infrastructure introduces substantial hurdles: Accelerator underutilization in RL : When you alternate between training and rollout generation, expensive GPUs and TPUs remain idle for most of the training run. Cache-blind load balancing : When you use standard Kubernetes round-robin and least-connections routing, multi-turn agent calls are scattered across arbitrary pods and wipe out key-value (KV) cache locality. Framework fragmentation : When you operate parallel, siloed compute clusters (such as bespoke Ray or Slurm setups) alongside Kubernetes, you fragment capacity and multiply maintenance toil. Agent security in multi-tenant clusters: When you execute untrusted, model-generated shell commands and scripts in shared environments, you expose clusters to sandbox escapes and privilege escalation. At KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 , Google Cloud is addressing these challenges by introducing and expanding a unified, open-source AI-native stack across Kubernetes and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) based on these components: OpenRL (CNCF Sandbox): A Kubernetes-native post training service that simplifies RL post-training and maximizes accelerator utilization. llm-d 1.0 (CNCF Sandbox): An open distributed inference control plane that provides prefix-cache-aware routing, disaggregated serving, and multi-tier KV cache management. Ray on GKE with KubeRay (CNCF Sandbox) : A framework that provides enterprise lifecycle management, elastic autoscaling, and Kueue -driven scheduling for distributed Ray compute and data processing. Agent Substrate (CNCF Sandbox) : An open orchestration runtime that provides lifecycle management and execution targets for multi-turn AI agent workflows. gVisor (CNCF Sandbox) : A kernel-level container sandbox that delivers strong system call isolation when you execute untrusted agent code in multi-tenant clusters. TorchTPU : A backend that provides first-class, native PyTorch support across Cloud TPUs and GPUs inside upstream vLLM and SGLang . Bridge reinforcement learning and Kubernetes with OpenRL While supervised fine-tuning (SFT) has become standard practice, domain excellence especially in multi-step reasoning, mathematical proofing, and autonomous tool use requires RL. Historically, it's been difficult to bridge the world of ML experimentation with production Kubernetes fleets. ML researchers want to iterate rapidly in Python and PyTorch by using standard reward functions, while platform teams need multi-tenant governance, quota enforcement, and predictable scheduling. To eliminate this friction, Google created OpenRL and contributed it to the CNCF Sandbox . Architectural highlights of OpenRL Clean 4-primitive Python abstraction : Researchers write standard Python training code that's centered around four core primitives ( forward_backward , optim_step , sample , and save_state ). OpenRL translates these primitives into Kubernetes scheduling workflows without requiring developers to learn Kubernetes internals or manage infrastructure code. Cooperative accelerator time-slicing : OpenRL interleaves training steps and rollout inferences on the same physical accelerators. This approach avoids the need to dedicate separate, static clusters to compute-bound training and latency-sensitive rollout generation. Delta-weight synchronization : Shipping full multi-gigabyte model weights over cluster networking after every optimization step creates massive network saturation. OpenRL transmits only parameter deltas to rollout workers, eliminating rollout cold starts. Zero-config dynamic resource allocation ( DRA ) : OpenRL automatically profiles model context lengths, batch dimensions, and LoRA versus full fine-tuning configurations. It then dynamically bin-packs workloads across a heterogenous accelerator fleet by using native Kubernetes DRA claims. Distributed inference at scale with llm-d 1.0 After you post-train a model, serving it serving it under interactive, bursty agent traffic presents a new set of distributed systems challenges. Standard ingress controllers treat LLM traffic as stateless HTTP requests, scattering sequential turns across different replicas and constantly rebuilding KV cache. Google Cloud, Red Hat, IBM Research, CoreWeave, and NVIDIA co-founded the project, with contributions from over 500 engineers across 25+ organizations. Today, llm-d 1.0 is the CNCF Sandbox distributed inference control plane that transforms standalone inference engines (like vLLM and SGLang) into a coordinated, cluster-wide serving fabric. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'apiVersion: inference.networking.x-k8s.io/v1alpha1

The Endpoint Picker evaluates real-time KV cache residency across worker pods. In production deployments, it's doubled KV cache hit rates from 35% to 70% and cut median time-to-first-token (TTFT) by 70-85% on multi-turn agent workloads. 3-Tier KV cache offload : When accelerator high-bandwidth memory (HBM) nears capacity during long-context interactions, llm-d cascades KV cache blocks from HBM → host CPU RAM → local NVMe SSD / Google Cloud Managed Lustre / Cloud Storage. This offload prevents expensive context recalculations. EPD Disaggregation with DisaggregatedSet : Decouples Encoding, Prefill, and Decode (EPD) onto specialized hardware pools that are connected by high-speed interconnects. DisaggregatedSet is built built on Kubernetes LeaderWorkerSet (LWS) . It enables independent horizontal scaling and coordinated, zero-downtime rolling upgrades. Native TorchTPU upstream support : PyTorch models run natively on Google Cloud TPUs inside upstream vLLM and SGLang through TorchTPU. Developers get day-zero parity across TPU v5e, v6e, and v7x alongside NVIDIA GPUs without the need to maintain private forks or rewrite pipelines. Latency-tolerant async processing & flow control : The llm-d-async-processor component pulls background, latency-tolerant tasks from Pub/Sub or Redis into cluster slack capacity. It applies strict traffic prioritization so background processing never degrades interactive user experiences. Fleet observability with Prism : Track cluster-wide throughput, inter-token latency (ITL), TTFT, and cache hit ratios by using Prism , the llm-d open-source benchmarking and performance dashboard. Distributed Python & ML orchestration with KubeRay While specialized runtimes handle inference and RL loops, distributed data preparation, embedding generation, and distributed PyTorch training depend heavily on Ray . KubeRay provides an open-source, Kubernetes-native operator that manages the complete lifecycle of Ray clusters, jobs, and services ( RayCluster , RayJob , and RayService custom resources) on Kubernetes. code_block <ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'apiVersion: ray.io/v1

Native Kueue queueing & multi-tenancy : KubeRay integrates directly with Kueue for multi-tenant fair sharing, priority preemption, and quota management across shared GPU and TPU capacity. Elastic autoscaling : KubeRay dynamically scales worker pods based on active Ray tasks and actor placement, preventing idle resource consumption. Strong isolation for AI agents: Agent Substrate & gVisor As multi-turn AI agents advance from conversational assistants to autonomous systems that generate code, execute shell commands, and orchestrate external APIs running untrusted, model-generated code in shared clusters introduces serious security risks. Google Cloud is contributing Agent Substrate and continuing core contributions to gVisor in the CNCF Sandbox: Kernel-level sandboxing : gVisor provides a user-space kernel that intercepts and virtualizes system calls, which helps ensure that untrusted agent code can't compromise the host kernel or access neighboring tenant workloads. Sub-second ephemeral execution : Sandboxes spin up in milliseconds per agent turn, providing isolated execution environments for both RL rollout generation in OpenRL and live production agent workflows. Proven in practice: Mastering domain reasoning To evaluate this complete open-source stack on a rigorous enterprise workload, we tested Gemma 4 against the open-source Legal Agent Benchmark (LAB) developed by Harvey.ai . This benchmark spans 24 complex legal practice areas from mergers and acquisitions (M&A)M&A due diligence to contract dispute analysis. The evaluation produced these results: Benchmark results : While standard SFT plateaued around 50% accuracy on multi-step reasoning rubrics, when we applied reproducible RL loops with OpenRL, we lifted model accuracy to 70% . Operational efficiency : The entire training pipeline dynamically shared GPU and TPU capacity with concurrent LoRA and inference jobs on GKE without manual partition management. title: New survey finds enterprises trapped between legacy software and AI modernization
raw_text: Throughout my career in cybersecurity and infrastructure protection — both in government and now at Google Cloud — I have consistently seen that friction between new and existing technology is often a barrier to progress. A new piece of software or service may work wonderfully on its own but then it’s placed within a complex, interconnected IT environment and lost in the operational inertia. Today, enterprise technology is experiencing a historic transformation. Organizations globally are moving beyond integrating AI and LLMs, and are now utilizing AI to power autonomous, agentic workflows. Nearly 90% of the Fortune 100 are already using Gemini Enterprise to build, scale and govern agents. But as AI systems begin to plan, execute multi-step processes, and work alongside human teams, leaders are confronting this same tension between cutting-edge and legacy technology. To understand how existing technology environments shape an organization’s ability to operationalize AI, Google Cloud partnered with Hypothesis Group to survey 1,250 enterprise IT and business decision-makers across the United States. The findings reveal a critical paradox: the legacy software systems enterprises rely on to deliver technology to their employees are simultaneously functioning as an innovation tax, actively holding back the AI transformation leaders are trying to achieve. Legacy IT’s operational toll In our study, we defined “legacy” technology as software running locally on computers and servers rather than natively in the cloud. Across industries, decision-makers report that maintaining this footprint exerts a constant friction on their AI ambitions. The consequences to AI are not theoretical. Nearly half (49%) of respondents report that relying on on-premises software has actively delayed, reduced in scope, paused or canceled AI or other technology initiatives. Digging deeper, routine patch application and maintenance emerged as a primary operational bottleneck. As AI-enabled vulnerability discovery accelerates, the rate at which flaws are surfaced in legacy codebases has outpaced what human security teams can realistically address. This creates a zero-sum game between routine maintenance of legacy systems and AI modernization. Instead of directing engineer cycles toward AI modernization, IT teams are spending their time and resources on maintaining legacy systems. Enterprise monoculture Why do organizations continue to rely on legacy environments that constrain their modernization? As our research shows, it is not necessarily architectural preference — but the result of vendor lock-in. Beyond narrowing technology choice, deep provider dependence introduces commercial constraints. In our study, 39% of decision-makers report that reliance on legacy software and cloud providers forces them to navigate complex licensing rules or contracts, or limited negotiating flexibility. Even more concerning is the systemic operational risk created by single-vendor concentration. Concentrating operating systems, productivity applications, cloud hosting and emerging AI models within a single vendor's monoculture creates an immense single point of failure. An autonomous AI agent is only as secure as the operating system and network it traverses. When that underlying stack is vulnerable, organizations are not deploying resilient intelligence; they are expanding their attack surface. Customer choice The solution to vendor lock-in is straightforward: enterprise buyers and policymakers must ensure organizations have genuine choice and interoperability in their software, cloud and AI architectures. Furthermore, 80% of leaders agree that a provider’s installed base should not determine which AI technology an organization uses, while 78% believe that the providers who led the previous era of enterprise technology may not be best positioned to lead the AI era. Organizations want the freedom to choose best-of-breed intelligence on its own merits, rather than accepting bundled defaults tied to legacy desktop software. Accelerate agentic technology Delivering this level of autonomous agility across the enterprise requires modern technology built to support the agentic era. Here are a few ideas to get there: Demand architectural and provider choice: AI and cloud must never be held hostage by the legacy software running local servers, email or desktop operating systems. Organizations need the commercial and architectural freedom to select best-of-breed IT on its own merits. Commit to secure-by-design foundations: The industry must move past the broken cycle of releasing insecure software and patching it after the fact. Software manufacturers must engineer durable, resilient architectures where entire vulnerability classes are eliminated before code ever ships — relieving understaffed IT teams from perpetual applying routine but necessary patches. Deploy AI-driven defense to remediate legacy debt: For the millions of lines of vulnerable legacy software already running in production, organizations must shift from manual triage to proactive, AI-assisted defense. By deploying platforms like Security Command Center and Mandiant threat analytics, teams can use intelligence to continuously surface active exploit paths, prioritize critical exposure and automate remediation across complex, hybrid environments. The promise of agentic AI is to help automate friction away, and accelerate human ingenuity. But that future cannot be built on top of software designed decades ago. As IT leaders plan their roadmaps, it is time to ask: Is your technology foundation accelerating your future, or are you paying a maintenance tax just to keep the past running? Learn more about the research here .
summary: Throughout my career in cybersecurity and infrastructure protection — both in government and now at Google Cloud — I have consistently seen that friction between new and existing technology is often a barrier to progress. A new piece of software or service may work wonderfully on its own but then it’s placed within a complex, interconnected IT environment and lost in the operational inertia. Today, enterprise technology is experiencing a historic transformation. Organizations globally are moving beyond integrating AI and LLMs, and are now utilizing AI to power autonomous, agentic workflows.

This year we’ve witnessed a fundamental change in cybersecurity. When the year began, only a few organizations were using LLMs and agents to find and fix vulnerabilities. Today, it’s happening at scale across enterprises. Organizations expected a reality with agentic hacking where scale, speed and sophistication would outpace human-only response; today, we’re seeing it in practice. Organizations predicted software development at an unheard of pace; today, we’re securing software delivered in hours and days instead of weeks and months. We have passed many milestones, and the world won’t go back — and we are all digging in to fully understand the new reality. The year ahead promises to be challenging, exciting, innovative and will outpace 2026. In the year ahead, enterprise software will change as agility and speed provided by agentic development shifts us from a collection of static applications to a live fabric of autonomous agents that can manage pricing, negotiate supplier contracts, allocate capital, and reroute supply chains in real time. To make this vision a reality, many organizations are rushing to build agents. It’s on us as an industry to ensure the development and operations models are designed to be trustworthy and safe. The risks in 2027 won’t be just server outages or stolen databases. As the agentic operations world takes off, we also need to be concerned about the data and technology foundation that agents rely on. When an agent makes a consequential decision, you must be able to reconstruct the entire story: what inputs came in, how the agent reasoned through them, which tools it called, what parameters it passed, and why policy allowed it. Without that trace, you can't debug it, you can't validate its correctness, and you can't trust it. And if you can't trust it, you can't scale it. Karthik Narain chief product and customer officer, Google Cloud Security must evolve to protect the balance sheet through decision integrity. Every consequential action taken by an autonomous system requires a complete, tamper-proof decision trace, recording and tracking: Inputs entered into the system. How the model reasoned through its decisions. Which tools the model called, what parameters it passed, and why policy allowed it. Collecting this data will help ensure that your teams can reconstruct, validate, and audit every automated decision before scaling. Making the alert queue disappear, from chasing tickets to setting doctrine For decades, security operations centers (SOCs) have suffered from crippling alert fatigue — too many alerts compounded by legacy security tools that hand human analysts half-finished investigations. When autonomous threats can probe a network and move laterally in minutes, human defenders can’t manually stitch together logs across eight different consoles or approve individual defensive actions at microsecond speed. 2027 is the year analysts stop chasing alerts and start shaping outcomes. Ramya Chitrakar vice-president, Engineering, Google Cloud Security That broken alert queue disappears in 2027 by flipping the operational model. The alert becomes the final output of an investigation. Autonomous defensive agents will handle the data enrichment, correlation, and triage automatically, surfacing a verified conclusion rather than a raw ticket. Instead of chasing alerts at a keyboard, human analysts move up the stack to set strategic doctrine, define risk appetite, and verify automated actions built for rapid explainability — where any defensive decision can be understood by a human in 60 seconds and reversed in 30. Moving Beyond Zero: Transaction-level trust and first-class agent identities As enterprises deploy thousands of custom agents across multicloud environments, flat trust architectures, shared human service accounts, and blanket administrator tokens are turning internal workflows into high-leverage entry points for prompt injection and lateral movement. Traditional Zero Trust is too rigid and broad to govern autonomous software acting on its own. We need to extend the Zero Trust concept, not just at the network layer and the machine layer, but now down to the transaction layer. Heather Adkins vice-president, Security Engineering, Google The year ahead demands an architectural shift to Beyond Zero so we can extend verification down to every individual transaction, network packet, and point-in-time authorization. Every autonomous agent should be treated as a first-class identity with its own verifiable credentials, strict least-privileged scope, and open communication standards. When backed by real-time autonomous reasoning, we can dynamically allow a transaction on Tuesday and block the exact same request on Wednesday if conditions look anomalous. Closing the loop between live runtime and defect-free code The traditional divide between writing software and securing it is breaking down, while adversaries actively target the open-source libraries and external tools that coding assistants pull into codebases. Developers can no longer file a ticket and wait weeks for a manual security review, yet deploying hasty, unvalidated automated patches in production is just as dangerous to business continuity as the vulnerability itself. Adversaries aren't just attacking model math and algorithms. They're actually poisoning the open source software, supply chain, MCP tools, and external libraries that agentic coding assistants pull automatically into code bases. Sandra Joyce vice-president, Google Threat Intelligence In 2027, security becomes a closed-loop, continuous system embedded directly into the software delivery pipeline. By placing agentic reasoning inside developer tools, we can perform threat modeling and catch configuration errors side-by-side as code is written. It’s also crucial that we link live production environments directly back to source code so that defenders can trace a real-world exposure to the exact line of code, validate whether it is genuinely exploitable, and deliver a pre-tested fix at machine speed without breaking production. Turning internal ground truth into a decisive defender advantage Concerns persist around attackers gaining the upper hand in cybersecurity, and many fear autonomous capabilities will only widen that gap in 2027. Adversaries are already compressing six months of reconnaissance into hours, and exploiting flaws before vendors even know they exist. Compounding the challenge for defenders, no single model can discover or patch every vulnerability across code and cloud on its own. The defender's advantage is that attackers operate with fragmented external visibility and guesswork. Defenders own the complete ground truth, identity privilege graphs, internal network architecture, code lineage, and real-time runtime activity. Sandra Joyce vice-president, Google Threat Intelligence In the year ahead, defenders will use autonomous technology to capitalize on the one thing an outside attacker will never have: complete internal ground truth. While adversaries operate with fragmented external visibility and guesswork, defenders own the full picture of their identity privilege graphs, internal network architecture, code lineage, and live runtime activity. By feeding that unified context into multi-model ensembles — such as pairing lightweight models for continuous scanning with deep reasoning models that cross-validate findings and eliminate false positives — organizations can spot and remediate toxic combinations of permissions and configurations that look harmless in isolation, before an external attacker can ever piece them together. Countering asymmetric threat speed and the new extortion playbook Not every adversary will embrace machine speed the same way in 2027. While state-sponsored espionage actors often avoid loud, hyper-fast automated scripts that risk triggering alarms and blowing their long-term stealth, cybercriminals tend to go all-in on autonomous velocity. What we're seeing right now is a variety of adversaries that are exploiting vulnerabilities before the vendors even know about it. Charles Carmakal CTO, Mandiant Consulting As endpoint defenses get better at blocking traditional file-encrypting ransomware, criminal crews are shifting to rapid, high-volume data theft and extortion — specifically targeting proprietary model weights, custom agent skills, prompt libraries, and cloud GPU compute (“ LLMJacking ”). Preparation here means eliminating security silos. It’s a critical failure point to treat models, agent permissions, software supply chains, and cloud infrastructure as separate domains. Instead, we want to unite them under a single, intelligence-led governance framework that allows defenders to lock down high-value autonomous assets and shut down extortion paths before data can leave the environment. Red-teaming the agentic enterprise before adversaries attack In the rush to capture productivity gains in the year ahead, many enterprises are deploying custom agents directly into core business workflows without testing how those systems behave under adversarial pressure. That mistake leaves guardrails vulnerable to bypasses, scanner blinding, and indirect prompt injection. One of the things that the team's been doing over the past few years is doing a lot of red team exercises… with those agentic solutions, so that we have the opportunity to identify and fix the issues before an adversary has the ability to do that against victim organizations. Charles Carmakal CTO, Mandiant Consulting Continuous, proactive adversarial red-teaming must be a mandatory prerequisite before any autonomous workflow touches production. Systematically attempting to break into agentic systems, bypass safety controls, and manipulate model behavior prior to deployment is crucial to securing the agentic era. Critically, model safety engineering should combine the results of those tests with frontline threat intelligence on novel attack prompts and evasion techniques. Defenders can then harden classifiers and neutralize new attack techniques before adversaries can use them against real victims. Orchestrating specialized agent teams to prevent agent sprawl Relying on a single generalist agent to defend an enterprise will fail in 2027 because deep technical skills do not transfer across domains. For example, an agent built to reverse-engineer malware is not the agent that should reason about an identity blast radius. As departments across the business rapidly spin up uncoordinated, standalone agents without centralized oversight, agent sprawl is emerging as the next iteration of shadow IT , threatening to derail enterprise agent deployments through inadequate governance. Technological adoption cannot outpace architectural governance… We have to prioritize machine speed defense. Security cannot remain a manual checkpoint that slows innovation down. Sandra Joyce vice-president, Google Threat Intelligence Just as a well-coordinated human team beats a lone generalist, the year ahead belongs to orchestrated networks of specialized hunter, decoder, and responder agents, each operating with its own domain depth, memory, and dedicated tools. Succeeding at scale requires building the governance and orchestration layer first. The key here will be to establish graduated autonomy, shared state, clean handoffs between specialized agents, and a central coordinator that knows precisely when to act autonomously and when to escalate to a human. title: Introducing TPU Sync: Fast KV cache and weight transfer for inference and RL on TPU
raw_text: As frontier AI evolves from stateless single-turn prompts to million-token agents, disaggregated serving, and continuous reinforcement learning (RL), the primary bottleneck in AI infrastructure has shifted from raw compute to orchestrating live model state — both the contextual state held in massive key-value (KV) caches during inference and the parameter state updated and broadcast from trainers to rollout samplers during RL. Whenever this state is trapped inside a single chip's memory or stalled on network transfers, AI accelerators sit idle. We designed TPU Sync from first principles to serve as the model-state layer across TPU clusters — built on the architectural insight that accelerator High Bandwidth Memory (HBM), host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network (DCN) should operate as a single, co-designed memory hierarchy. An open-source, native C++ library, TPU Sync moves TPU-tiled tensors directly across this hierarchy with asynchronous DMA transfers that overlap data movement with active computation. For inference, it decouples TPU compute from network backpressure and turns host DRAM, local SSDs, and Google Cloud Managed Lustre into an automated, multi-tier KV cache; and for RL, it exposes low-level DMA and DCN primitives that higher-level RL frameworks can use to stream updated weights from trainers to samplers. By accessing device buffers in place rather than copying or locking them, TPU Sync consistently slashes KV transfer latency by over 90% and reduces Time to First Token (TTFT) by an average of 90% for heavyweight open-weight MoE models (235B–480B parameters) in prefix-caching and disaggregated-serving workloads, compared to running without TPU Sync. Across this shared model-state layer, TPU Sync integrates directly into existing infrastructure stacks across PyTorch (via TorchTPU ) and JAX — serving as the TPU KV cache connector for vLLM, SGLang, and llm-d disaggregated serving, while providing low-level transfer primitives for Pathways and multi-controller JAX (McJAX) RL pipelines. Understanding TPU Sync: The kitchen analogy To understand TPU Sync’s impact, imagine a high-end restaurant kitchen. Think of the TPU as an incredibly fast executive chef working on a tiny countertop (the chip's HBM). When preparing a massive feast, the chef needs lots of ingredients (the KV cache), which quickly clutter the counter. The standard kitchen (without TPU Sync): When the small counter fills up, the chef has to toss out prepped ingredients and chop them again from scratch the next time an order needs them — stalling the kitchen on repetitive prep work (prefill recomputation). The upgraded kitchen (with TPU Sync): TPU Sync adds a spacious side pantry (pinned host RAM), a shared walk-in cold storage room accessible to every station in the kitchen (shared cluster storage), and a coordinated team of runners. The runners slide full prep trays directly between the counter, the pantry, and peer stations without repacking them (direct DMA in native TPU layout). Crucially, the runners swap trays in and out while the chef keeps cooking (asynchronous, non-blocking transfers). Key use cases for TPU Sync TPU Sync improves system throughput and latency in workloads requiring deep context, high concurrency, multi-turn reasoning and RL rollouts: Long-context AI agents and multi-turn chats : When interacting with an AI agent over an extended 256K to 1M+ token session or analyzing massive documents, the model generates a continuously growing KV cache. Instead of allowing this state to exhaust HBM capacity, TPU Sync automatically tiers older KV blocks out of TPU HBM and into large pools of host RAM (with experimental tiering to shared secondary storage). Enterprise applications with heavy system prompts (prefix caching): AI serving platforms receive thousands of queries that share common instructions or documents. Rather than recomputing prefixes that the model has already processed, TPU Sync extends the prefix cache into distributed host memory so concurrent sessions can reuse precomputed KV blocks and bypass redundant prefill computation. Disaggregated serving architecture (prefill/decode): In modern enterprise deployments, workloads are isolated: Compute-bound nodes process the initial massive prompt (prefill), while memory-bound nodes draft the response token-by-token (decode). TPU Sync bridges this hardware gap by acting as a high-bandwidth Host-to-Host (H2H) streaming pipeline. It routes the processed context directly from the prefill nodes to the decode nodes, consistently delivering an over 90% reduction in data transfer overhead. Reinforcement learning pipelines (experimental): Validated on internal RL workloads and included in the repository as an experimental module, TPU Sync provides low-level DMA and DCN transfer primitives that higher-level RL frameworks can use to synchronize model weights between trainers and inference samplers — including automatic resharding across different trainer and sampler parallelism layouts — to reduce the time rollout workers spend waiting on weight updates. Breaking through the memory wall with TPU Sync At its core, TPU Sync establishes a high-performance data transfer path between TPU HBM and host RAM, as well as across TPU hosts via the DCN. It achieves this through four key architectural advantages: Layout-preserving direct DMA with in-place buffer aliasing : TPU Sync accesses the underlying JAX PJRT buffers or PyTorch tensors in place and moves slices directly between TPU HBM and page-locked ( DmaMap -registered) host memory in a single hardware DMA. By keeping tensors in their native TPU physical tile layout across HBM, host DRAM, storage, and the wire, data lands ready for immediate Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU) execution with no Python serialization, no layout conversion, and no user-space bounce buffers. Compute-overlapped transfers : Rather than taking an exclusive lock or making an on-device copy of static KV cache and weight buffers, TPU Sync creates raw PJRT buffer aliases ( PJRT_RawBuffer ) without holding PJRT usage locks so block-level transfers can run concurrently with active in-place computation, with built-in DMA pacing to keep large transfers from delaying kernel launches. No XLA compilation in the data path : Because TPU Sync executes transfers and tile-aware strided resharding in native C++ outside the XLA graph, moving KV blocks or resharding weights across different trainer and sampler topologies does not trigger runtime compilation — keeping the data path fast and framework-agnostic. High-bandwidth PCIe DMA and DCN streaming : Using the raw_transfer library’s direct PJRT raw-buffer DMA pipeline, TPU Sync reaches up to 223 GB/s of aggregate D2H and H2D throughput per Ironwood (TPU v7x) host out of the 256 GB/s PCIe Gen5 hardware ceiling, and streams across the DCN at up to ~192 Gbps on a single 200 Gbps NIC (or ~350 Gbps across dual 200 Gbps NICs with NUMA-aware multi-NIC striping). TPU Sync exposes a low-level data transfer API, making it easier for developers to integrate high-speed TPU data transfer into higher-level frameworks. Higher-level architecture Built on top of its core transport and resharding primitives, TPU Sync provides a modular orchestration stack for distributed cache management: Global KV store: A global registry that maps prompt prefix hashes to physical cache blocks, handles dynamic lookups, and coordinates LRU eviction and tier demotion. TPU Sync controller: The orchestration layer that generates transfer plans, coordinates data movement across nodes, and handles lease management and recovery. KV cache manager: The local execution engine that tracks block states, manages HBM, host DRAM (including /dev/shm warm-boot persistence) alongside experimental POSIX storage backends, and executes asynchronous DMA transfers. Figure 1. TPU Sync operates as the model-state layer on TPU, unifying TPU HBM (Tier 1), pinned host DRAM (Tier 2), shared storage (Tier 3), and multi-host DCN under a single layout-preserving DMA data plane. Solving disaggregated serving and prefix caching Let us take a closer look at how TPU Sync helps with some of the use cases we listed in the earlier section. By treating host pinned memory as a substantial, high-speed Tier 2 cache, TPU Sync reduces the fragmentation and memory limits of standard HBM setups. Prefill/Decode (P/D) disaggregated serving In state-of-the-art serving topologies, prefill (compute-bound) and decode (memory-bound) phases are isolated on separate node pools. To prevent latency bubbles, TPU Sync bridges this gap with a highly optimized, three-step pipeline: Direct-DMA offloading: Once a prefill node processes an initial prompt, TPU Sync immediately moves the resulting KV blocks into pinned host RAM via its asynchronous D2H DMA path. Host-to-host streaming : The TPU Sync controller then orchestrates a high-bandwidth Host-to-Host (H2H) transfer, streaming the context directly to the assigned decode node. Overlapped ingestion : As blocks arrive in the decode node's host RAM, TPU Sync triggers an asynchronous H2D transfer directly into TPU HBM. This happens concurrently with active decoding computation, substantially minimizing TTFT. Host-powered prefix caching For highly concurrent systems sharing large system prompts or running multi-turn agentic loops, TPU HBM is not large enough to hold multiple active cache blocks. TPU Sync extends the prefix cache out of HBM (Tier 1) into substantial, distributed host RAM pools (Tier 2). Because TPU Sync transfers are asynchronous, it overlaps the PCIe DMA loading of the next required prefix from host RAM with the compute of the current request — minimizing TPU idle time between requests. For workloads that exceed even host DRAM capacity, TPU Sync also includes an experimental POSIX storage backend (Tier 3+) that asynchronously spills older KV blocks to local SSDs or shared Google Cloud Managed Lustre storage — pairing with llm-d prefix-affinity routing on GKE so replicas can recall cached prefixes across tiers without recomputing prompts. Sample performance results P/D disaggregated inference result highlights: Over 90% KV transfer overhead cut : For heavyweight models like Qwen3 235B, median KV transfer latency dropped from several seconds down to a flat ~230 ms. Substantial TTFT reduction : Demonstrated an average of 60% reduction in TTFT for heavyweight models (Qwen3 235B) under controlled, low-concurrency testing benchmarks, and an average of 90% for 480B under low concurrency. Substantial high-traffic scalability : During sustained traffic spikes, TPU Sync achieves an average of 30% to 70% increase in token output throughput for 235B, depending on traffic distribution. Prefix caching result highlights: Expands KV cache capacity beyond HBM : When heavyweight MoE model weights consume most of device HBM, on-chip memory can hold only a few long-context prefixes. Offloading into pinned host DRAM expands effective cache capacity by an order of magnitude. Sustains high cache-hit rates under concurrency : Pooling distributed host RAM keeps shared system prompts and multi-turn agent contexts warm across thousands of concurrent sessions instead of thrashing HBM. Significantly reduces prefill recompute : Directly bypasses heavy compute layers for repeated instruction blocks and system prompts, reducing average TTFT by up to 90% on 64K-context workloads while delivering over 50% higher throughput and a 30% reduction in P99 inter-token latency (ITL). Please see the note 1 below on the testing configuration. Ecosystem adoption and partnerships TPU Sync serves as the open, composable memory substrate across our PyTorch-on-TPU and Kubernetes serving ecosystem, built in close collaboration with key open-source maintainers and infrastructure partners: Inferact (vLLM-TorchTPU) : Co-engineered with Inferact, maintainers of vLLM-TorchTPU , TPU Sync is integrated directly via vLLM's native KVConnector interface. It powers Direct-DMA host DRAM offloading and multi-host P/D disaggregation across frontier open-source models. RadixArk (SGLang-TorchTPU) : In partnership with RadixArk, maintainers of SGLang-TorchTPU , TPU Sync serves as both the high-speed P/D disaggregation transfer backend and the native I/O backend for SGLang’s hierarchical cache. llm-d 1.0 integration : llm-d 1.0 pairs with TPU Sync on GKE to deliver global prefix-cache-affinity routing, per-rank decode session pinning, and experimental two-stage capacity spill to Google Cloud Managed Lustre. Validated by frontier AI labs and enterprises : Frontier AI organizations are already adopting our PyTorch-on-TPU serving stack and evaluating TPU Sync multi-tier architectures for production deployments — including Meta, alongside major enterprises like Wayfair, and multi-silicon partners. Get started TPU Sync is available today as open source with Python wheels for both PyTorch ( tpu-sync-torch ) and JAX ( tpu-sync-jax ), and is integrated with vLLM-TorchTPU , SGLang-TorchTPU , and llm-d on GKE. Visit the GitHub repository to explore the architecture docs, C++ and Python APIs, and deployment guides. We are committed to working with the open-source community to advance the model-state layer on TPU — supporting new frontier architectures, expanded storage tiering, and longer-horizon agentic and RL workloads. For more up-to-date performance results, please see our ongoing efforts on public benchmarks ( InferenceX ). 1. Performance results are based on internal testing conducted in July 2026 on TPU v7x (2x2x1 topology), configured with PCIe Gen5 (x16) per TPU chip and one or two 200 Gbps NICs enabled per host, running tpu-inference v0.24.0 (using JAX 0.10.2 and libtpu 0.0.42.1). Metrics presented represent average and median performance improvements observed under controlled laboratory conditions. Actual real-world performance, cache hit rates, and latency reductions will vary based on system configuration, network bandwidth, concurrent traffic, and specific user workload patterns.

title: Now generally available: GKE dynamic slicing for higher resilience, and efficiency for TPUs
raw_text: Running large-scale AI workloads on TPU and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) requires infrastructure that adapts as fast as your models change. Dynamic Slicing is generally available on GKE, which decouples logical TPU slice formation from physical nodepool provisioning. Compared to creating a static nodepool for each TPU slice, dynamic slicing reduces AI workload startup times by up to 5x and workload recovery by 4.5x — maximizing TPU goodput, efficiency, and workload resilience at scale. Beyond one workload, one nodepool Previously, managing TPU capacity at GKE standard required separate, fixed TPU slice topology nodepools, increasing startup times and complexity while preventing multi-host nodepools from hosting multiple AI workloads. Changing workload needs meant manually deleting and recreating nodepools. Additionally, this tight coupling created large failure domains where a single hardware fault crashed an entire slice, slowing recovery while reprovisioning. To overcome these challenges, we built GKE dynamic slicing, which decouples physical hardware provisioning from logical slice formation, dynamically stitching together TPU cubes using TPU optical circuit switching (OCS) technology to form various larger slice topologies (super-slicing), or partitioning TPU cubes into smaller slices for multiple workloads to run inside a nodepool (sub-slicing). By enabling workloads to assemble custom TPU slice topologies on demand without having to delete and recreate static nodepools, dynamic slicing reduces job startup latency, limits the blast radius of hardware failures, accelerates recovery of workloads, and improves fleet utilization and efficiency. Dynamic slicing delivers several key improvements for platform teams: Zero-downtime topology agility: Completely eliminates the rigid "delete-and-create" nodepool cycle, allowing to dynamically stitch together TPU cubes (16 VMs nodepools) to form large TPU slices, or carve out smaller-slices on the fly as an AI workload is submitted. Up to 5x faster job startup: Slashes job startup times by up to five times by instantly assembling logical slice topologies from pre-provisioned TPU nodepools instead of waiting for a slow, new nodepool deployment. Improved fleet utilization: Improves resource efficiency and eliminates idle capacity by enabling multi-tenant packing of smaller workloads within nodepools. Additionally, it lets you provision partially healthy nodepools. This way, you can utilize healthy hosts that would otherwise be unavailable. Up to 4.5x faster recovery and fault tolerance: Accelerates recovery by isolating large slice failures to a TPU cube (a 16-VM 4x4x4 slice topology) and swapping unhealthy cubes in one to two minutes. Enhanced visibility and control: Offers comprehensive insight into potential TPU partitions (slices) within each cube, covering real-time health and usage metrics to facilitate proactive, optimized workload scheduling. Dynamic slicing architecture GKE dynamic slicing is offered in two forms: super-slicing, to create larger scale TPU slices that exceed the size of a single TPU cube; and sub-slicing, which provisions smaller, independent slices from a single cube. Dynamic super-slicing GKE dynamic super-slicing utilizes TPU optical circuit switching (OCS) technology to dynamically connect TPU cubes (consisting of 16 VMs configured in a 4x4x4 slice topology) at the time of workload scheduling. By altering the OCS network configuration dynamically, larger slice topologies are created and tailored to the workload slice needs outlined in the Kubernetes workload manifest, significantly enhancing operational efficiency. Super-slicing fundamentally relies on a baseline conversion of all available TPU capacity into uniform nodepools composed of 16-VM (4x4x4) TPU cubes. When a TPU slice topology is specified in Kubernetes workload YAML file, the GKE scheduler (or your custom scheduler) identifies the request and instantiates slice creation. This process uses the TPU optical circuit switch to stitch multiple 4x4x4 cubes together, dynamically instantiating the targeted slice topology and scheduling the workload directly onto the newly established super-slice. How a 4x4x16 super slice (comprising 64 Ironwood VMs and 256 total chips) is formed using four Ironwood cubes (also provisioned as GKE nodepools). At runtime, the slice is created dynamically by stitching together the TPU network across all TPU chips in these four cubes. Dynamic sub-slicing Dynamic sub-slicing partitions a single, pre-provisioned TPU cube (16 VM nodepool) into smaller, independent sub-slices on demand. You can manage a single pool of uniform TPU cubes and partition them on demand. With this approach, multiple distinct jobs with completely different slice topology requirements can run concurrently and fully isolated inside the same physical TPU cube, boosting overall resource utilization and allowing you to salvage and run workloads on healthy partitions, even if a portion of the cube is unhealthy. When a workload is scheduled, sub-slicing dynamically parses its specific slice topology requirements from the incoming Kubernetes manifest. It then locates healthy partitions within the cubes, activates the high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnect (ICI) network to form sub-slices, and deploys the workload onto the newly created slice. Upon workload completion, the scheduler automatically deconstructs ("deforms") the slice and returns the partitions to the shared pool, making them immediately available for future workloads without having to recreate the GKE nodepool. How GKE sub-slicing dynamically partitions a 16-host TPU cube into smaller, independent slices (e.g., 2x2x4 with 16 chips down to 2x2x2) for optimal utilization of TPU resources. Customer use cases You can leverage dynamic slicing to form massive TPU slice topologies to meet large scale training, ranging from large 8,000-chip single slices to multi-slices of multiple thousands of chips, down to single-host four-chip configurations. This supports a wide variety of heterogeneous AI workloads within the same environment. Designed for the demands of largest-scale workloads, dynamic slicing delivers resiliency and operational efficiency for AI workloads running across thousands of accelerators. Sub-slicing offers the versatility to efficiently scale inference workloads ranging from small to large-scale deployments. Dynamic slicing scheduler for GKE GKE provides deployable schedulers optimized for dynamic slicing, or you can use your own custom scheduler to manage workload placement. This flexibility allows for intelligent workload scheduling based on proactive health status monitoring. See more in our documentation . Getting started Pre-provision nodepools To get started, you must perform a one-time activity of pre-provisioning TPU capacity into nodepools of 16 VMs each (maps to a TPU cube or sub-block). This baseline conversion allows for dynamic stitching of these units into custom slice topologies on demand. Dynamic slicing introduces a new type of nodepools called an incremental provisioning nodepool. An incremental provisioning nodepool is a fault-tolerant model that supersedes the traditional "all-or-nothing" approach for creating TPU slices. GKE provisions the nodepool using all available healthy hosts even if some hosts in a 4x4x4 (16 VM) slice are faulty. The system continuously reconciles state, automatically adding pending nodes once faulty hosts recover. This setup is a prerequisite for dynamic sub-slicing, as it allows the high-speed ICI network mesh to be dynamically configured. By using incremental provisioning, you can create nodepools for your entire capacity at once, reducing operational toil and maximizing TPU utilization by enabling sub-slicing on healthy nodes. Workload scheduling on dynamic slicing After enabling the slice controller in the GKE cluster and configuring the GKE scheduler, you can indicate the need for dynamic slices for your workloads using simple workload annotations. Upon detecting these annotations, the scheduler automatically triggers the GKE slice controller to create a Slice Custom Resource (CR) to form the dynamic slice at runtime. Once the slice is formed, the workload is scheduled on the dynamic slice. Refer to documentation for examples. Repair When host or network failures disrupt workloads, the GKE scheduler maintains resilience and continuous operation through targeted recovery strategies: Super-slicing (slices larger than 1 TPU cube): Hardware failures are isolated to a smaller unit — the TPU "cube" — allowing the scheduler to quickly reform the slice by removing the unhealthy cube and choosing all healthy cubes. Sub-slicing: Slices on faulty infrastructure are dynamically reformed using available healthy partitions. Next steps Dynamic slicing (super-slice and sub-slice) is available for TPUs and is offered in all regions where TPUs are available. It is supported exclusively in TPU All Capacity under reservation mode. For working examples of dynamic slicing, refer to the documentation .
summary: Running large-scale AI workloads on TPU and Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) requires infrastructure that adapts as fast as your models change. Dynamic Slicing is generally available on GKE, which decouples logical TPU slice formation from physical nodepool provisioning. Compared to creating a static nodepool for each TPU slice, dynamic slicing reduces AI workload startup times by up to 5x and workload recovery by 4.5x — maximizing TPU goodput, efficiency, and workload resilience at scale. Beyond one workload, one nodepool Previously, managing TPU capacity at GKE standard required separate, fixed TPU slice topology nodepools, increasing startup times and complexity while preventing multi-host nodepools from hosting multiple AI workloads.

title: Our newest TPUs: 8tx and 8i Max, built for the agentic era
raw_text: Editor’s note: This blog was originally published on News from Google . We first designed TPUs more than a decade ago motivated by Google’s internal demands, including voice recognition and language translation. Eight generations of TPUs later, the use cases have exploded, covering: i) training and serving our own Gemini models, ii) agentic workloads, iii) delivering services to Google Cloud customers on our cloud infrastructure, and most recently, iv) allowing customers to deploy TPUs directly into their own data centers. TPUs are now a rapidly growing business with nearly 100 customers — including frontier labs, trading firms, retailers, universities, and more. At Google Cloud Next in April, we introduced two new specialized TPUs in the same generation — 8t for large-scale training and 8i for real-time reasoning. TPU 8t and 8i offer up to 2.7 times better training performance and 80% better inference price performance, respectively, versus our previous generation of TPUs. Today, we’re taking that a step further , expanding our eighth-generation TPU portfolio with two additional systems: TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack, and TPU 8tx for secure and confidential inference . This is the first time we have introduced four TPU systems in a single year. Our expanded eighth-generation TPU portfolio: TPU 8t, TPU 8i, TPU 8tx, and TPU 8i Max. While we’ve always co-designed our TPUs in partnership with Google DeepMind, we’re now increasingly getting feedback from external organizations on their specific needs. With computing moving from human to agent scale, businesses are asking for accelerators that can reason across AI models’ massive context windows. In addition, some highly regulated customers are asking for specialized encryption capabilities for unique workloads. The new TPU systems we are announcing today address this new reality. Coupled with our recent PyTorch announcements , our aim is to make TPUs more easily accessible to every developer and Cloud customer. By combining modular custom silicon with an open and easy-to-use software stack, we can deliver new hardware and system configurations at the pace of the AI industry. Building the computer around the chip Today, we’re announcing two new TPU systems — and there’s an important difference between a new chip and a new system. Designing a new chip means laying out billions of microscopic transistors on a silicon wafer in a multi-year process bound by the laws of physics and a complex, long-duration manufacturing lifecycle. A system, on the other hand, is about how we bring together the compute, networking, and storage around the chip. This can include how they are packaged with the chips, to quickly meet emerging customer needs and research use cases. When we built our very first TPU more than a decade ago, we knew AI software would evolve much faster than silicon manufacturing ever could. So we made a foundational bet on system balance and modularity, architecting our TPUs as building blocks as part of our AI Hypercomputer , so engineers could rapidly adjust packaging, high-speed memory, optical networking, and security around them. That approach allows us to deliver specialized supercomputers in a matter of months rather than years. Specializing for secure, high-context AI Each system in our eighth-generation TPU portfolio targets a distinct part of the AI lifecycle. TPU 8t and TPU 8i established the baseline for this generation of chips: TPU 8t was designed to be a training powerhouse for massive foundation models with maximum “goodput” — or the useful intelligence delivered per watt of energy used. TPU 8i is the reasoning engine, designed to break the memory wall, cutting inter-chip communication delays by up to half. Now, as enterprises bring autonomous agents into production, we have created two new configurations of these foundational systems to solve two urgent new challenges: hardware-level data security and million-token context scale. TPU 8tx TPU 8tx, our third eighth-generation system, is optimized for secure and confidential inference and is also great for small-scale training. It’s built for regulated enterprises and governments running frontier or proprietary models and autonomous agents alongside their most sensitive data. Normally, data is encrypted when stored or sent over a network, but has to be unlocked in memory while a computer processes it. Built on the same silicon as TPU 8t and paired with 5th Generation AMD EPYC CPU hosts, TPU 8tx builds security directly into the hardware layer, keeping sensitive data and model weights protected and isolated even while in active use. And by adopting the same low-latency Boardfly network we created for real-time reasoning, TPU 8tx keeps multi-step agents moving, delivering up to 2x lower latency compared to TPU 8t with a near-zero performance penalty. Pairing training-grade compute with a fast inference network also means organizations can simultaneously run and customize their models on a single system. TPU 8tx enables teams to fine-tune models using their private data, distill large models into smaller ones, and train their agents through reinforcement learning, all without needing to migrate sensitive data between separate clusters. Designed for sensitive enterprise workloads, TPU 8tx provides hardware-level confidential compute for private fine-tuning and secure agent execution. TPU 8i Max Our fourth system, TPU 8i Max, is built for a different problem: the memory wall. When dozens of AI agents work together across an entire software codebase or hours of video at once, memory bandwidth quickly becomes the bottleneck. So we took two low-latency TPU 8i chips and combined them onto a single package. TPU 8i Max scales compute and memory in lockstep, delivering double the compute, double the SRAM and double the HBM bandwidth of TPU 8i, so processors remain equipped with essential data and so that large workloads do not stall. Further, because TPU 8i Max fits twice the silicon within the existing rack footprint, data centers can deploy significantly more computing power per square foot and per watt. The dual-chip TPU 8i Max system, engineered for massive context windows and maximum compute density. While flexible across workloads, together the four systems in our eighth-generation TPUs give customers a purpose-built accelerator for every stage of the agentic lifecycle. TPU 8t for scale-up training, TPU 8i for low-latency reasoning, TPU 8tx for confidential computing, and TPU 8i Max for massive context windows and the highest compute density per rack. Opening up TPUs to every developer When we launched the first TPU more than a decade ago, there were only a handful of companies running workloads that needed the processing power of a TPU. The use cases were specialized, so engineers would use optimized frameworks and hand-tuned code. Over the years, as AI has advanced, more and more companies began using accelerators. Now, AI adoption is at a point where TPUs are excellent for a wide range of companies and use cases, and as a result, we’ve been working systematically to remove barriers to adoption so that TPUs are as easy-to-use as general-purpose hardware. This investment comes together today across these key areas: Opening up TPU development to every PyTorch developer; no code rewrites needed: Last month, we open-sourced TorchTPU , so PyTorch code and Hugging Face models now run natively on TPUs, alongside out-of-the-box TPU backends for leading open-source inference engines like vLLM and SGLang. And to make hardware optimization effortless, our new open-source TPU agent suite (now in preview) plugs directly into coding tools like Claude Code, Cursor, and Google Antigravity to automate TPU onboarding in minutes, diagnose bottlenecks, and autotune custom kernels using plain language. For production deployments, our new open-source XLA Serving Engine lets you train models in Python and serve them directly in a low-latency C++ runtime across TPUs, GPUs, and CPUs. Industry-leading production performance on InferenceX and AgentX benchmarks: In production, what really matters is outcomes on real AI workloads rather than theoretical peak chip speeds. On industry-standard InferenceX and AgentX benchmarks , which test realistic agentic coding and long-context work, our native vLLM-TorchTPU software stack on TPUs achieved state-of-the-art price-performance marks. New evaluations demonstrate these advantages extend across a wide range of frontier open models and open-source serving stacks while maintaining high model accuracy. Upcoming software optimizations on this same hardware will drive those results even further. Eliminating idle compute waste for autonomous agents: Because AI agents are stateful, they frequently pause for seconds or hours while waiting on a database lookup, an external software tool, or human feedback. To make our agents more resource-efficient during those pauses, our new Agent Compute Engine software automatically suspends and resumes idle sessions, cutting operational infrastructure costs. Breaking through the memory wall with the model-state layer ( TPU Sync ): Building the computer around the chip also means unifying memory, storage, and networking in software. As agents reason across million-token contexts and continuous reinforcement learning (RL) loops, memory quickly becomes the bottleneck. We’re open-sourcing TPU Sync , the model-state layer for TPU clusters. TPU Sync turns chip HBM, host DRAM, shared storage, and the data center network into a single, co-designed memory hierarchy — automatically tiering massive KV caches off the chip in milliseconds, streaming context across disaggregated prefill and decode nodes, and synchronizing RL weights to cut KV transfer latency and Time to First Token (TTFT) by more than 90%. Scaling distributed workloads across TPUs from a single controller: Now generally available on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Cloud Pathways brings the Google DeepMind runtime behind Gemini to every Google Cloud customer. Using a single-controller architecture and pathwaysutils , you can orchestrate large-scale TPU systems across multiple slices as if they were one local machine for pre-training, reinforcement learning, and multihost inference. Cloud Pathways keeps long-running jobs moving through hardware disruptions with colocated Python sidecars, sub-minute slice hot-swapping, and elastic resharding. Stitching custom TPU topologies on-demand with GKE dynamic slicing: Now generally available, GKE dynamic slicing decouples physical hardware provisioning from logical slice formation using optical circuit switching (OCS) technology. By dynamically assembling TPU cubes into larger topologies (super-slicing) or partitioning them into smaller, isolated workloads (sub-slicing) on-the-fly, this update completely eliminates rigid, manual nodepool recreation cycles. This topology agility slashes job startup times by up to 5x and accelerates fault recovery by up to 4.5x, maximizing overall fleet utilization and workload goodput across all TPUs. Co-designing with a decade of experience Shipping four TPU systems and a unified, open software stack in a single year only happens when silicon architects, networking engineers, compiler teams, and Google DeepMind researchers build side-by-side. Increasingly, we’re even tapping into AI to ideate and build the next generation of AI infrastructure. From using Google DeepMind’s AlphaChip reinforcement learning system to using Gemini to deliver chip layouts in hours rather than weeks, we’re using TPU-powered AI services to rapidly accelerate next-generation TPU hardware development. This is true co-design and a unique Google differentiator. Learn more about our new TPU systems by tuning into today’s broadcast at 9 a.m. PT.

title: Cloud Pathways, a distributed ML runtime for massive accelerator fleets, now GA
raw_text: Today, we are thrilled to announce the general availability (GA) of Cloud Pathways ( Pathways on Cloud ) on Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) as a core runtime pillar of the Google Cloud AI Hypercomputer . Originally engineered by Google DeepMind to train and serve Google's frontier models — including Gemini — Pathways is our distributed machine-learning runtime designed for massive, heterogeneous accelerator fleets. In fact, over the last 90 days alone, leading AI companies and global enterprises have processed more than 130 million Cloud TPU chip-hours using Pathways on GKE, across a broad range of TPU generations. With Cloud Pathways, every Google Cloud customer can use the same single-controller runtime, colocated Python sidecars, and elastic fault tolerance that power Google's largest AI workloads. We are also pleased to announce a Preview integration with Cluster Director to extend Cloud Pathways to Slurm clusters, supporting unified multi-slice JAX execution, elastic training, and interactive notebooks. What is Cloud Pathways? As AI workloads scale across thousands of accelerators, spanning multi-slice pre-training, disaggregated inference, and multi-program reinforcement learning (RL) loops, traditional multi-controller setups become harder to program and manage. In default multi-controller JAX, every TPU host runs its own separate Python interpreter with only a localized view of its connected devices and executes the same SPMD program in lockstep, making heterogeneous MPMD workflows and cross-slice resource management complex and brittle. Cloud Pathways replaces multi-controller management with a unified single-controller architecture built on the open-source Interim Framework Runtime (IFRT) . By setting JAX_PLATFORMS=proxy with pathwaysutils , a single JAX client process views and orchestrates multiple large TPU slices, spanning thousands of TPU chips as if they were all connected locally. Learn more about Pathways in our latest deep-dive blog here. Core architectural innovations Cloud Pathways has the following features: Single-controller orchestration: In Cloud Pathways, a single controller manages graph evaluation, persistent Cloud Storage compilation caching, and asynchronous XLA HLO dispatch across TPU slices. Colocated Python sidecars: Client-side colocated Python sidecar containers (with shared-memory support) let you run compute-intensive Python logic such as distributed data loading and checkpointing directly on TPU hosts. Resilient and elastic training: Cloud Pathways decouples job survival from individual slice interruptions with elastic training ( pathwaysutils ) using host-memory snapshots to dynamically reshard training down to N-1 slices during hardware failures without crashing the client. Interactive mode and Shared Pathways Service: Run, inspect, and debug JAX workloads interactively from a notebook or terminal using interactive mode , or share a long-running pool of Cloud TPU slices on demand across multiple users and jobs with the Shared Pathways Service. Proven enterprise impact and customer momentum Frontier AI labs, quantitative research firms, and global consumer platforms have adopted Cloud Pathways to run mission-critical production workloads on GKE, including: Hyperscale multi-host inference: One of the world's largest consumer technology companies runs production batch and reinforcement learning (RL) inference on Cloud Pathways across tens of thousands of TPU v5p , Trillium (v6e) , and Ironwood (TPU7x) chips, consuming over 100 million chip-hours per quarter, and co-designed elasticity primitives with Google to expand into pre-training. Elastic pre-training and multi-host RL for scientific foundation models: Google Cloud customer ZenteiQ uses Cloud Pathways on GKE with Cluster Toolkit ( gcluster ), colocated Python sidecars, and host snapshotting to scale elastic pre-training ( MaxText ) and single-controller reinforcement learning ( MaxText + Tunix ) across multi-slice Trillium ( v6e ) clusters for its scientific foundation models. "Running multi-day pre-training and post-training jobs on high-cost accelerators requires reliable continuity through both unexpected hardware faults and planned maintenance windows. By running Cloud TPUs and MaxText with Cloud Pathways on the Google Cloud AI Hypercomputer stack, ZenteiQ relies on a proven controller that monitors our TPU topology and dynamically re-meshes and resizes the workload whenever a chip or slice goes offline. Combining Pathways with host snapshotting in production pushes recovery time down to a minimum when disruptions occur, keeping our available TPU capacity fully utilized with very little stall time. Our ML engineers no longer have to spend their hours watching job health or managing manual restarts, and can stay focused on their research workloads." - Prof. Sashikumaar Ganesan, Founder, ZenteiQ Getting started with Cloud Pathways Cloud Pathways is generally available today in all Google Cloud regions supporting Cloud TPU v5e , TPU v5p , Trillium (TPU v6e) , and Ironwood (TPU 7x) on GKE, with versioned container images ( us-docker.pkg.dev/cloud-tpu-v2-images/cloud-pathways ) supporting JAX 0.10.1+ . Cloud Pathways is also available in Preview on Slurm TPU clusters in Cluster Director . To start building with Cloud Pathways: Read the overview: Explore the Introduction to Pathways on Cloud in the AI Hypercomputer documentation. Deploy your cluster: GKE: Follow the step-by-step guide to Create a GKE cluster with Pathways using Cluster Toolkit ( gcluster ) or the gcloud CLI. Slurm: Deploy Pathways via Cluster Director using the step-by-step guide . Run your workloads: Dive into our production guides for Batch workloads , Interactive notebook mode , Resilient & elastic training , Multihost inference , Porting JAX workloads , and Troubleshooting .

title: Microsoft’s AI bug hunter finds Rust flaw that went undetected for nearly 11 years
raw_text: Microsoft researchers have uncovered a memory-safety bug in Rust’s standard library that had gone undetected for nearly 11 years, alongside other flaws that can trigger undefined behavior even in applications written entirely in safe Rust. Two of the findings affect stable Rust, including a separate issue that could cause applications to access freed memory. The nearly 11-year-old bug involves Rust’s process::exit function. Microsoft’s FORGE Lab researchers found that calling the function from a child thread could cause the runtime to remove the main thread’s alternate signal stack while it was still running. If the main thread subsequently experienced a stack overflow, the operating system could be unable to deliver the signal correctly, resulting in a segmentation fault instead of Rust’s intended stack-overflow handling. “The process::exit signal stack bug was in the standard library for nearly 11 years,” the researchers wrote in a blog post . Microsoft said the researchers found no reliable exploitation path under the conditions they examined and assessed practical exploitation as unlikely. The research used Hyenas, FORGE Lab’s AI-powered vulnerability-scanning system, to investigate unsafe code in Rust’s standard library. Hyenas is the lab’s research version of codename MDASH, Microsoft’s agentic vulnerability-discovery system. Microsoft said some of the bugs were found with help from Hyenas. Researchers then examined the underlying code, reproduced the issues, assessed their security impact, and reported them to Rust maintainers. Microsoft said the practical risk is limited. Each flaw requires unusual conditions to trigger, and a bug in the standard library becomes “a serious vulnerability only if a real program reaches the API in that way,” the researchers wrote. Unsafe code challenges Rust’s safety guarantees Rust’s ownership model and type system are designed to prevent memory-safety problems commonly associated with languages such as C and C++. However, its standard library relies on unsafe code internally for operations that the compiler cannot verify. Components such as Vec and String use these operations but expose them through safe APIs. Microsoft said these APIs must meet a strict soundness requirement: “no matter how safe code uses it, it must be impossible to trigger undefined behavior.” Microsoft grouped the findings into three categories: unsafe code that assumes operations will not panic, code that trusts user-provided implementations to behave correctly, and code that makes incorrect assumptions about the underlying system. The first involved a panic-safety problem in Rust’s MapWindows::clone implementation. The function created a buffer before fully initializing its contents and then called a user-provided clone operation to populate it. If that operation triggered a panic, Rust’s unwinding mechanism could invoke the buffer’s destructor, which would attempt to access uninitialized memory. Microsoft said the reported fix prevents the partially initialized buffer from being destroyed before initialization is complete. Another finding involved str::replace. The researchers found that the function could make an incorrect assumption about a custom implementation of the nightly Pattern trait. A custom implementation could supply a non-ASCII byte where the code expected an ASCII character, causing the replacement operation to produce invalid UTF-8 data. Subsequent string operations could then trigger undefined behavior, Microsoft said. System-level bugs affect stable Rust Microsoft said the first two categories of weaknesses were already being studied in 2021 through Rudra, a static analyzer developed by members of the research team. The standard library had also addressed panic-safety problems as far back as 2015, but similar weaknesses continue to appear in its implementations. The third category involves interactions between Rust and underlying operating systems and C libraries. Besides the process::exit issue, researchers identified a problem in Rust’s CommandExt::exec functionality involving the process-wide environment variable array. Microsoft found that the function could modify this shared state while holding a read lock, potentially allowing other threads to access inconsistent data. Under certain conditions, concurrent operations could leave the environment pointer referencing freed memory. Microsoft said both the process::exit and CommandExt::exec findings affect stable Rust. A proposed fix for the environment-variable issue, which avoids modifying the shared array by calling execve directly, was under review when the blog was published. Two issues reported by Microsoft’s team remained open at publication. The blog also discussed related reports from other researchers and fixes still under review. Findings feed into Microsoft’s security products Microsoft said the research findings can also feed into Microsoft Perception, its multi-agent security system, where specialized agents work across broader security workflows. It would therefore help the company improve the development of MDASH, which brings agentic vulnerability discovery into Microsoft Defender. For example, Microsoft’s Web App Pen Test Agent can use MDASH findings to prioritize testing, assess exploitability against live applications, and provide information to support remediation, the researchers wrote. “Our goal isn’t to simply find more bugs,” the researchers wrote, but to identify meaningful issues and improve the safety of foundational software developers and organizations depend on. The Rust project had not responded to a request for comment from CSO at the time of writing.
