title: Qubole supply chain attack exposed AWS, Entra ID, and Okta credentials
raw_text: An attacker has abused AWS cross-account IAM roles to access multiple customer environments, steal data, and harvest credentials in a supply-chain attack that ran between October 14 and October 26. Researchers from Wiz, working with Sentra and Mandiant, said they observed an attacker using IAM credentials for Qubole’s AWS account to assume roles in customer environments. The compromised credentials allowed the attacker to access customer AWS accounts that had previously established cross-account access permissions with Qubole. The access was used to enumerate cloud resources, retrieve secrets and configuration data, download files from Amazon S3 , and test credentials belonging to affected organizations. Sentra, which initially identified suspicious activity across several customer environments, said the campaign affected dozens of Qubole customers. The attacker was said to have exploited integrations that remained trusted even after some organizations had stopped using the platform. Attackers used Qubole’s AWS credentials Qubole integrations rely on cross-account Identity and Access Management ( IAM ) roles. Customers typically create roles that allow identities belonging to Qubole’s AWS account to assume them, with an External ID serving as an additional check against unauthorized access. The attacker had credentials that could satisfy this requirement. Wiz said the first suspicious activity was observed on October 14, when an IP address associated with Mullvad VPN attempted to assume customer integration roles from AWS account 805246085872, which Qubole uses for its platform operations. The requests used an IAM user identified as AIDA3W7DIFLYOLTK63SFS. Most of the activity that came later originated from an OVH-hosted VPS, 57.129.54[.]120. The attacker also began using a second IAM identity associated with Qubole’s AWS account on October 18, alongside another Mullvad VPN address. All malicious role-assumption requests identified by Wiz included the required External ID and succeeded. Many of the targeted roles had seen no legitimate Qubole activity during October, but their permissions remained active. After gaining access, the attacker enumerated cloud resources, including S3 buckets, databases, EC2 instances, security groups and IAM identities. The intruder also accessed AWS Secrets Manager, Systems Manager Parameter Store and Lambda function configurations to retrieve credentials and other sensitive information. Attackers stole data, and hosted a suspicious Linux image The attacker used the assumed roles to download data from Amazon S3, enumerating accessible buckets and objects before retrieving their contents. In some instances, Wiz said, entire buckets were downloaded in individual sessions. Credentials discovered in the compromised environments were subsequently tested using TruffleHog, a secrets-scanning tool. These included AWS access keys, Microsoft Entra ID service principal credentials and Okta OAuth client credentials. Sentra reported identifying more than 100 passwords and keys read within minutes, alongside thousands of additional credential records contained in downloaded files. The company also said the attacker performed no write operations in the observed environments, suggesting an operation focused on data theft. Wiz also found a bootable Linux ISO image, named “sso_agent.iso,” hosted on the attacker’s OVH infrastructure. The image collects system information, communicates with the server over TCP port 23458, and can execute remotely supplied shell commands. Its configuration suggests it may have been designed to target Windows systems, the researchers said in a blog post . Wiz, however, did not find any deployments of the image and could not confirm whether it had been used against victims. The campaign has not been attributed to a known threat group. Tightening integrations and third-party access will help Wiz recommends that organizations using Qubole review AWS CloudTrail records dating back to October 1, 2026, across all accounts containing integration roles. Investigators should look for suspicious AssumeRole activity originating from Qubole’s AWS account, particularly requests from non-AWS infrastructure and IAM identities identified in the disclosure. Subsequent activity involving Secrets Manager, Parameter Store, Lambda and S3 should also be investigated, Wiz noted. Other recommendations include removing unused third-party integrations and narrowing trust policies to specific vendor IAM principals rather than allowing an entire external AWS account to assume a role. Organizations should also restrict role assumption to documented vendor network ranges using AWS source IP or VPC endpoint conditions.
summary: An attacker has abused AWS cross-account IAM roles to access multiple customer environments, steal data, and harvest credentials in a supply-chain attack that ran between October 14 and October 26. Researchers from Wiz, working with Sentra and Mandiant, said they observed an attacker using IAM credentials for Qubole’s AWS account to assume roles in customer environments. The compromised credentials allowed the attacker to access customer AWS accounts that had previously established cross-account access permissions with Qubole. The access was used to enumerate cloud resources, retrieve secrets and configuration data, download files from Amazon S3 , and test credentials belonging to affected organizations.

title: Anthropic sharpens AI coding and security capabilities with Mythos 5.2
raw_text: Anthropic has introduced Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, claiming significant improvements in handling complex software engineering tasks while cutting API prices by 20% compared with the previous versions. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 share the same underlying model but have different safeguards. Fable is broadly available, while direct access to Mythos is restricted to vetted cybersecurity and life sciences organizations to limit potential misuse. The models are both priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, down from $10 and $50, respectively. Anthropic said the newer versions can generate output up to 30% faster than their predecessors. The company reported substantial gains in coding performance. Fable 5.2 scored 49.1% on the FrontierCode 2.0 benchmark at its Xhigh effort setting, compared with 32.4% for Fable 5.1. The benchmark assesses whether maintainers of open-source projects would accept AI-generated changes to their code. Performance and costs could entice enterprises The models’ improved performance and lower prices could make long-running AI agents viable for software migrations and scientific research, according to Lian Jye Su , chief analyst at Omdia. Higher task completion rates could further reduce deployment costs, he said. Anthropic said Fable 5.2 at its “High effort” setting achieved a coding benchmark score comparable to Opus 5.5 at its highest setting, at roughly half the cost per task. The comparison suggests that Fable could be more economical for some demanding assignments, although the savings would depend on the workload and effort setting. “Anthropic has cut the price of a token, not the price of a thought,” said Sanchit Vir Gogia , chief analyst at Greyhound Research. He urged CIOs to treat AI processing effort as a budget consideration and measure costs against successfully completed tasks. Anthropic also recommends Opus 5.5 for most coding and knowledge work, with Fable and Mythos intended for more demanding assignments. Reliability challenges persist In an internal experiment, an Anthropic engineer tasked Fable 5.2 with building a prototype operating system. The model coordinated more than 1,000 subagents over eight days and produced software that could boot on a laptop. Su said the improvements bring enterprises closer to highly autonomous software development, although widespread deployment will depend on addressing persistent operational limitations. “Reliability remains an issue without human supervision,” Su said. Coordinating multiple AI agents across enterprise tools and internal teams also remains difficult, he added. Organizations will need to monitor agent activity and run these systems in appropriately isolated environments. Critical changes should remain subject to human approval , with sufficient visibility into agent behavior to support audits. Pareekh Jain , CEO of Pareekh Consulting, said complex legacy systems and the need to meet business requirements could limit how much software development enterprises can delegate to AI agents. Faster vulnerability discovery raises concerns Anthropic said Mythos 5.2 identified 89.6% of vulnerabilities in its internal CVE Rediscovery evaluation, compared with 78.3% for Mythos 5.1. Conducted against 1,829 previously disclosed vulnerabilities, the test assessed whether models could independently rediscover flaws in software snapshots taken before the vulnerabilities were fixed. The company said Mythos 5.2 was also better at reproducing vulnerabilities and developing fixes. Anthropic has restricted direct access to Mythos 5.2 through its verification programs. However, Claude Enterprise customers can use the model’s vulnerability detection capabilities through Claude Security without joining those programs, the company said. According to Su, “Mythos 5.2 shifts the balance towards defenders in controlled enterprise settings.” Jain, however, cautioned that advances in AI-powered vulnerability discovery could also help attackers identify software weaknesses more quickly. “This creates an AI-powered race between attackers and defenders,” he said. Data retention raises compliance questions Anthropic said customers eligible for zero data retention can continue using Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 under those arrangements, while other customers face 30-day retention for safety monitoring. The company has also introduced Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, currently in private beta, which allows automated safety monitoring to run on prompts and responses stored within customers’ infrastructure. Gogia said data retention requirements could outweigh the benefits of lower API prices for regulated enterprises. He urged procurement teams to obtain written confirmation of zero-retention arrangements before deploying the models for sensitive workloads. The article originally appeared on InfoWorld .
summary: Anthropic has introduced Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2, claiming significant improvements in handling complex software engineering tasks while cutting API prices by 20% compared with the previous versions. Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 share the same underlying model but have different safeguards. Fable is broadly available, while direct access to Mythos is restricted to vetted cybersecurity and life sciences organizations to limit potential misuse. The models are both priced at $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens, down from $10 and $50, respectively.

title: When everything is a threat, nothing feels safe
raw_text: When you leave home, you lock the door. When you get into the car, you fasten your seat belt. These are familiar safety habits. We understand their purpose, know how to perform them and rarely need to stop and think about them. Our digital lives are different. We shop, bank, work and keep in touch with family and friends online, often without clear signs of where a danger begins or which precaution matters most. We receive a steady stream of warnings about new scams, stolen credentials, data breaches and software vulnerabilities. The messages vary in urgency, but many seem to demand our immediate attention. The result can be an uncomfortable contradiction: information intended to make us safer can also leave us overwhelmed and less willing to act. In conversations with people inside and outside the technology field, I keep hearing variations of the same concerns. There is a new scam every week, and no way to keep up. If major companies can be breached, how can an individual protect themselves? Almost anything done online seems risky. These are reasonable questions. As a cybersecurity professional, I believe our response should go beyond repeating that threats exist. We need to help people understand which risks are relevant, what they can do about them and where their responsibility ends. When a warning becomes background noise There are good reasons to monitor the threat landscape. Criminals adapt their techniques, fraud schemes evolve and vulnerabilities sometimes require urgent remediation. Ignoring those developments is not a sensible strategy. But a threat’s existence is not the same as a person’s or organization’s exposure to it. A vulnerability described as critical does not necessarily create the same level of risk for every business. The answer depends on which products are in use, whether affected systems are exposed, what safeguards are already in place and the potential business impact. A critical flaw in technology that an organization does not use may be worth noting without requiring emergency action. A less dramatic issue affecting a business-critical, internet-facing service could deserve immediate attention. The headline alone cannot make that distinction. Yet headlines are often how people encounter cybersecurity. When warnings arrive without context, prioritization or practical guidance, they compete for a limited amount of attention. What should be exceptional starts to feel routine. An alert that genuinely requires action may disappear into the noise. There is a meaningful difference between staying informed and feeling compelled to remain on high alert every moment of the day. Security fatigue is not simply a lack of interest Researchers have a name for part of this experience: security fatigue . In a 2016 qualitative study, researchers at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) interviewed 40 everyday computer users about security and privacy . Signs of fatigue appeared in 25 interviews, even though fatigue was not the study’s initial focus. Participants described frustration with repeated requirements and advice, along with feelings of resignation and diminished control. The researchers connected these experiences with decision avoidance, choosing the easiest option available, and disregarding protective guidance. The study was small and qualitative, so it should not be treated as a measure of how widespread fatigue is today. Its value lies in explaining behavior that security teams may otherwise label as carelessness. When someone dismisses yet another warning, they may not be indifferent to security. They may simply have lost the ability to tell what matters, what is urgent and what action is expected of them. This distinction matters for security leaders. If every message is marked urgent, we should not be surprised when urgency stops working. More warnings are not automatically better communication. Replace headline volume with decision criteria I do not believe people need to memorize every new phishing technique or follow every vulnerability disclosure to practice sound digital security. Nor is it sustainable for security teams to treat every issue as equally important. A better approach starts with three questions whenever a new alert appears: 1. Does this affect me or my organization? Is the alert about a service, device, account or process I use or oversee? 2. Does it require action now? Is there credible guidance and a concrete reason for urgency, or is this general information about a possible threat? 3. What is the most effective action available to me? Should I install an update, verify an unusual request through another channel, enable a safeguard or notify the appropriate team? This is not a guarantee of safety. It is a way to separate useful information from noise and preserve attention for decisions that matter. For individuals, a consistent baseline is more valuable than trying to recognize the scam of the week: keep devices and applications updated, use long and unique passwords with a password manager, enable multifactor authentication and verify requests that demand immediate action or sensitive information. These habits are easy to describe, even if implementing them sometimes requires help. For organizations, the equivalent is a risk-based process that connects alerts to actual assets, exposure, business priorities and clear owners. A security bulletin should answer who is affected, what the organization knows, what needs to happen and by when. When no action is required, saying so is also useful. The burden cannot rest entirely on users It would be unfair to finish this discussion by giving people another long list of obligations. If staying secure requires every employee to interpret technical warnings, navigate confusing settings and make the correct choice every time, the design of the system is part of the problem. Organizations and technology providers should make secure behavior easier by default. That includes sensible protective settings, automated updates where appropriate, effective filtering, straightforward reporting channels and clear instructions when a real decision is necessary. It also means preparing for mistakes through detection, response and recovery rather than assuming flawless human behavior. NIST’s work on human-centered cybersecurity makes a similar case : systems and guidance should account for people’s actual needs, capabilities and limitations. The goal is to make safe actions easier to take in practice, not merely to issue more instructions. Security leaders can put that principle to work by reviewing the warnings employees receive. Are several teams sending overlapping messages about the same threat? Do alerts explain the action and its owner? Are we asking employees to solve problems that technical control could prevent? Can people report a suspicious message without fearing blame? These questions recognize that user behavior matters, but it always takes place within a system that can support or undermine good decisions. Build awareness through confidence I want security awareness to treat people as partners, not as the weakest link to be frightened into compliance. Good risk communication should explain why something matters, whom it affects and what realistic next step is available. It should also be able to say when there is no reason to panic. Confidence does not mean assuming nothing will go wrong. It means understanding the most relevant risks, knowing which protections are in place and knowing where to turn when something unusual happens. We should therefore be careful about how we measure awareness. The number of alerts distributed, or training messages delivered tells us little about whether people can act on what they have learned. I would rather ask a more demanding question: After receiving our guidance, are people better equipped to make a sound decision? If the answer is no, we need to change how we communicate cybersecurity. Awareness should not be about frightening people. It should provide knowledge, a sense of control and practical ways to act.
summary: When you leave home, you lock the door. When you get into the car, you fasten your seat belt. These are familiar safety habits. We understand their purpose, know how to perform them and rarely need to stop and think about them.

title: SonicWall releases patches for 7 flaws in its firewalls, most involving unauthenticated access
raw_text: SonicWall on Monday updated its advisory about seven cybersecurity holes affecting its Gen 7 and Gen 8 firewalls, five of which allow unauthenticated remote attacks, to warn that it is aware of “potential” active exploitation of at least one of the bugs, CVE-2026-19868, a bypass of SAML authentication controls in its SonicOS SSL VPN service. And Frank Dickson , principal analyst at Dickson Research, pointed out that these flaws involve different SonicWall product lines to those recently reported . “The July zero-day and the September holes hit SonicWall’s SMA 1000 remote access appliances,” he said. “This one hits SonicOS, the operating system on its Gen 7 and Gen 8 firewalls. The pattern has jumped product lines. That makes it a vendor issue, not a product issue. Credit where due: SonicWall flagged the exploitation report in its own advisory and the fix shipped with the disclosure.” The seven vulnerabilities are: CVE-2026-107155, a permissive cross-domain policy vulnerability, with a CVSS score of 8.8; CVE-2026-107154, a session validation vulnerability, also with a CVSS score of 8.8; CVE-2026-82308, a pre-authentication heap buffer overflow vulnerability in SSL-VPN, with a CVSS score of 7.5; CVE-2026-19868, an authentication enforcement vulnerability via alternate authentication methods, with a CVSS score of 7.1; CVE-2026-77708, a pre-authentication stack buffer overflow vulnerability in TACACS+, with a CVSS score of 5.9; CVE-2026-77709 , a pre-authentication heap buffer overflow vulnerability in TACACS+, with a CVSS score of also 5.9; and CVE-2026-19703, a weak password hashing hole with a CVSS score of 5.2. SonicWall only provided a workaround for one of the bugs, CVE-2026-19868; it involves disabling or deleting any active LDAP, RADIUS, and TACACS+ authentication server configured on the firewall. A ‘mixed bag’ Dickson said the newly reported holes are a mixed bag. “SonicWall’s advisory rates its SAML bypass, CVE-2026-19868, a 7.1, below two 8.8 management interface flaws,” Dickson said. “Yet it is the one CISA added to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day SonicWall disclosed it. SonicWall describes ‘potential exploitation’ but CISA says active. I would listen to CISA.” The bug lets anyone holding valid credentials for another login method, such as a local account or LDAP, skip SAML and the MFA that rides on it, he noted, adding “companies moved their VPNs to SAML precisely so every login passes through the identity provider and its MFA prompt. This flaw breaks that promise.” Some of the other authentication holes are potentially less severe, however. “Three are pre-authentication buffer overflows whose stated impact is denial of service. They knock the VPN offline but they do not open it,” Dickson said. “The two 8.8 flaws work only under specific conditions. None of the six is known to be exploited. They matter, [but] they are not the headline.” Could be combined Sav Wheeler , malware research engineer at Malwarebytes, added that even though some of these holes do not appear to be especially serious on their own, they could be combined to be much more dangerous. “These scattered vulnerabilities at various stages of the authentication process combine to form a pathway where an attacker can bypass authentication almost entirely to penetrate a system and steal credentials,” Wheeler said. “The weak password hashing is a cherry on top for attackers that have already gained an initial foothold.” He sees CVE-2026-19868 as “the biggest individual vulnerability” because the potential MFA bypass through alternative authentication means that “the entire trust boundary of MFA could be effectively nonexistent even when an organization depends on it for security.” He noted, however, that although the attacker does need valid credentials for an alternate authentication method for this to work, “otherwise it requires little effort and resources to gain access, as they’re not compromising the MFA itself. Combined with the use of IP addresses for validation (CVE-2026-107154), which itself provides little security, this is a serious failure of authentication policy to ensure a user is who they claim to be.” Sanchit Vir Gogia , chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said that the biggest danger is when SAML sits atop older directory logins that stay live. “Remote access is the lifeblood of a distributed business, and one stolen directory password now reaches it. CISOs who rolled out SAML to end password-only access have cause to feel let down. SonicWall owes them a full account of how the second path stayed open.” A vendor risk management issue These continuing SonicWall vulnerabilities are a real issue, although the September and October flaws sit in another product, Gogia said. “Those hit the SMA1000 remote-access gateway, while this advisory covers SonicOS firewalls. But thirteen of SonicWall’s twenty entries in CISA’s exploited list carry the flag for known ransomware use, the highest share among eight edge vendors.” Dickson noted that the next steps for enterprise CISOs are trickier because the fault here might lie less with a vendor than with the product category itself. “The internet-facing VPN appliance is the Achilles’ heel of the perimeter, whoever builds it,” he pointed out. “Swapping vendors swaps one heel for another. The pattern should change how CISOs deploy the edge, not just whose logo is on it. Ask SonicWall whether these are new bugs or the same bug classes coming back.” However Erik Avakian , technical counselor at Infotech, said he was less willing to let SonicWall off the hook that easily. “Any vendor can and is generally going to experience vulnerabilities, but when we see repeated critical security issues affecting the same vendor that represent a pattern, particularly involving authentication and internet-facing infrastructure, it raises legitimate questions about their secure development practices, quality assurance, and the effectiveness of their own internal vulnerability management processes,” Avakian said. “At some point, this becomes more than just an individual vulnerability management issue. It becomes a vendor risk management issue.” He noted that CISOs need to evaluate whether the frequency and severity of these vulnerabilities are creating an unacceptable level of recurring exposure for their organization. “That doesn’t automatically mean replacing SonicWall products, but it does require holding the vendor accountable for improvement and to demonstrate their ability to address the underlying problems,” he said. Additional preventive measures In addition, Dickson suggested other ways CISOs can protect themselves in light of these new holes, beyond the obvious step of patching them. “List every way the VPN can authenticate a user: local accounts, LDAP, RADIUS, and TACACS+. Delete what you do not need, especially leftover local admin and service accounts. Rotate passwords on every non-SAML account that remains,” he advised. “Compare VPN logins against identity provider sign-ins. A VPN session with no matching SAML sign-in is your red flag. Look back as far as your logs go, since SonicWall has not said when exploitation began. And take the management interface off the open internet.”

title: Microsoft’s email security is unexpectedly blocking legitimate business mail
raw_text: Microsoft’s email filters meant to protect users from malicious messages appear to be rejecting legitimate ones. Over the last few days, some mail sent to Microsoft consumer addresses have bounced if they did not publish a domain-based message authentication, reporting, and conformance (DMARC) record. This includes messages to Outlook, Hotmail, Live, and MSN. The refusals began November 5 and are ongoing as of publication time . Microsoft did not announce a policy change and has not published a postmaster notice, service-health entry, or other blog post. The issue may indicate that a policy change and a bug may both be in play, noted Frank Dickson of Dickson Research. “Requiring every sending domain to prove it is who it says it is makes email safer,” he pointed out. “Doing it without notice, with an error message that points at the wrong problem, makes a mess.” Intermittent sending issues DMARC is meant to protect against spoofing, phishing , and business email compromise. Microsoft has had a rule in place since May 2025 requiring DMARC, but only from domains sending more than 5,000 messages a day to consumer mailboxes. But as of November 5, mail from small, ordinary senders, rather than from bulk ones, have been bounced due to lack of DMARC, Sender Policy Framework (SPF), or DomainKeys Identified Mail (DKIM). Senders have been receiving Non-Delivery Reports (NDRs) citing 550 5.7.1 or 550 5.7.23 errors, but are doing so inconsistently; some messages are getting through while others are rejected. For instance, one user reported this error message on Microsoft’s community forum : Your message to @hotmail.com couldn’t be delivered. hotmail.com couldn’t confirm that your message was sent from a trusted location. Another user reported the same problem, adding: “Some emails work fine and others return errors with SPF failed.” Adding to the confusion, some bounced domains were reported to have working SPF, DKIM, and DMARC. A Microsoft external staff moderator called it a “service degradation” currently under active investigation. According to email security company MailRoute , enterprises can determine if their domain is impacted with this command on any terminal (replacing example.com with their domain): dig +short TXT _dmarc.example.com . A response starting with v=DMARC1 means there is a DMARC record; no reply means there isn’t, MailRoute said. The fix is a single TXT record: v=DMARC1 ; p=none . This declares that a domain uses DMARC and asks receivers to send reports, but it tells them to take no action on failures, MailRoute explained. DMARC meant to make impersonation difficult DMARC relies on two foundational email authentication tools that must be active on a domain: SPF and DKIM. SPF verifies whether the sending server’s IP address is allowed to send email on behalf of a domain, while DKIM adds a cryptographic signature to the message to prove it wasn’t altered along the way and actually belongs to the domain it says it is coming from. DMARC checks the two, identifying whether the domain listed on the “from” address aligns with the validated domains. It ties those checks to the name the reader actually sees and tells receivers what to do with forgeries, Dickson explained. “Without it, impersonating your domain is easy,” he said. “That is where a lot of phishing and business email compromise starts.” But because Microsoft, at least to this point, has only required DMARC for larger senders, it is not standard across the board; many small senders reasonably concluded it did not apply to them, Dickson noted. This includes SMBs, nonprofits, schools, and professional practices such as law firms, accountants, and doctors’ offices running on domains that “someone set up years ago, and nobody has touched since.” Larger organizations miss DMARC on secondary domains, regional domains, and the subdomains that their marketing and billing platforms send from for mundane reasons. No one owns the domain name system (DNS), and “people fear breaking legitimate mail sent by third parties,” Dickson said. Quiet, inconsistent failure As MailRoute pointed out, what makes this particular malfunction so dangerous is its inconsistency: The person who sent the message sees a bounce “full of acronyms, assumes a glitch, and moves on.” Meanwhile, the customer never knows a message was sent. It fails quietly, which is “the bane of an email marketer’s existence,” Dickson said. Customers, patients, job applicants, and others use Hotmail, Outlook, Live, and MSN, and when invoices, password resets, appointment confirmations, and offer letters go missing, the customer thinks they’re being ignored, not necessarily that the message is not getting through. The good news is that the failures are findable, he pointed out. Every rejection generated a bounce, and bounces are logged. Enterprises should search mail logs, email platforms’ bounce reports, and help desk tickets for entries citing “ Message lacks SPF/DKIM/DMARC ” since Nov. 5. Then, resend what matters, time-sensitive transactional mail first. From there, fix the cause by confirming that every domain sending mail as you publishes a DMARC record, Dickson advised. If one is missing, a basic monitoring record (p=none) stops these bounces without changing how anyone else treats your mail, as long as SPF or DKIM lines up with the From domain. Microsoft 365 customers who never turned on DKIM for their own domains should do it now, he advised. “Do not rewrite SPF just because the bounce blames it,” he said. If your records are clean and mail still bounces, send the full bounce to Microsoft so it lands in the investigation. However, a p=none record is “first base, not home plate,” he said. The goal is p=reject , which tells receivers to refuse anyone forging your name. Inventory every service that sends email as you, Dickson advised: The CRM, the billing system, the HR platform, and the marketing tools. “Most organizations cannot produce that list,” he noted. “You cannot protect a domain when you do not know who is speaking for it.” A signal of what is to come While it remains to be seen what is causing this glitch, enterprises should make no mistake about where things are heading, Dickson said: DMARC will be enforced for every sender. Google and Yahoo began requiring it of bulk senders in February 2024; Microsoft followed in May 2025. “Requirements start with the big senders and then become the floor for everyone,” he said. “The rollout was botched, but the destination is not in doubt.” But while Microsoft has the destination right, “nobody should learn about a new rule from a bounce message.” This article originally appeared on Computerworld .
summary: Microsoft’s email filters meant to protect users from malicious messages appear to be rejecting legitimate ones. Over the last few days, some mail sent to Microsoft consumer addresses have bounced if they did not publish a domain-based message authentication, reporting, and conformance (DMARC) record. This includes messages to Outlook, Hotmail, Live, and MSN. The refusals began November 5 and are ongoing as of publication time .

title: The code and the court: Why your email security thinks like Napoleon
raw_text: In 1804, Napoleon gave France a code that much of the world still runs on. The Code civil replaced a tangle of local customs with a single written statute: orderly and knowable. In that tradition, the judge’s job, in Montesquieu’s phrase, is to be the mouth of the law, nothing more. Certainty was the point. Certainty has a cost. A codified system is only as current as its code. When the world produces something the code did not anticipate — a new technology, a new fraud — there is no statute to apply, and everyone waits for someone to write one. Your email security works exactly this way. That is the problem. Security by statute A signature is a statute. Someone observes an attack, writes a rule that describes it, and from that moment you are protected against that attack and its close relatives. It is fast, certain, and blind to anything the code has not been written to see. Signatures alone were never enough, so the industry made the code bigger. Anomaly detection and behavioral models are a thicker statute book, trained on what already happened and scoring how far a message deviates from it. More sophisticated than a signature, but not a different philosophy. A zero-day is a crime with no statute. The strongest evidence against codified defense is not the attack that fails a check. It is the attack that passes every one. When a supplier’s mailbox is compromised, the message arrives from a real domain, with valid credentials and earned reputation. Every check comes back clean because the infrastructure is genuine. Verizon’s 2026 Data Breach Investigations Report found that breaches involving a third party now account for 48% of the total, up 60% in a single year. Authentication did exactly what it measures : it confirmed the letter came from who it said, and had no rule for whether it should be believed. The code was consulted. The code said valid. The message was a theft in progress. Attackers understand this. A codified defense is cheap to walk around. You do not break the code; you do something it was never written to cover. The FBI’s 2025 Internet Crime Report put business email compromise losses above $3 billion in a single year, much of it carried by messages that broke no rule because no rule described them. The other tradition The English-speaking world chose a different system. Common law does not always wait for the legislature. A judge facing a situation no statute anticipated can reason from principle and precedent to a verdict. It adapts case by case. It is not simply a code that has to be rewritten. It is a court that knows how to weigh a new set of facts. That is the difference between detecting and reasoning. The fair objection is that a reasoning system also learns from the past. True. But there is a difference between matching a case to a stored pattern and applying a principle to a case you have never seen. A judge who has never encountered your particular dispute still knows how to weigh evidence. None of this means throwing out the code. Most mail is open and shut and should be settled that way in milliseconds. You keep the fast rule for the easy calls and save a full hearing for the contested ones. A court can also answer a question a code struggles with: why. A codified system can say “this matched” or “this deviated.” A verdict can cite its evidence: what the sender actually is, whether the relationship supports the request, what the message is asking for. You do not have to trust the reasoning. You check the evidence, because a ruling stands or falls on whether its facts hold up, not on the private thoughts of the judge. It is the opposite of a black box: a decision you can read, challenge, and overturn. None of this retreats from zero trust. Zero trust governs access, who gets in and what they can touch, and assumes nothing. This is about the verdict, whether a message is what it claims to be, and there the posture is not to presume guilt or innocence but to let the evidence decide. The court of last resort For the highest stakes matters, a mature legal system does not let the machinery decide alone. In security, some decisions belong with the person whose money is about to move. When a message asks for a wire, a change to vendor banking details or a payroll redirect, the right design does not render a silent verdict and hope. It escalates and asks the owner to approve the action itself. Reasoning handles the general docket. The human is the court of last resort, reserved for the decisions that deserve one. Match the process to the stakes. No analogy is perfect. Real judges in both traditions do more than this, and civil-law systems evolve through their own doctrine. The question worth ending on For most of this industry’s history, there was no choice, because machines could apply a code but could not weigh evidence and reason for a judgment. That is no longer true. There is a simple way to find out which system you are running. Ask your team how many attacks that reached a user came from infrastructure you already trust: a compromised vendor, a real account, a genuine DocuSign or Microsoft notification bent to a purpose it was never meant for. If that number is high, your defenses are not failing to enforce the code. They are enforcing it perfectly; against threats the code was never written to describe. So, the question is not whether your defenses are up to date. A code is always, by definition, up to date with yesterday. The question is whether your security is a code or a court, and whether it can rule on the case it has never seen, because that is the only case that was ever going to hurt you.
summary: In 1804, Napoleon gave France a code that much of the world still runs on. The Code civil replaced a tangle of local customs with a single written statute: orderly and knowable. In that tradition, the judge’s job, in Montesquieu’s phrase, is to be the mouth of the law, nothing more. Certainty was the point.

title: 7 tips for achieving defensive agility
raw_text: Defensive security agility reflects an organization’s potential to rapidly detect, adapt, and respond to evolving cyber threats and vulnerabilities without disrupting core operations. By abandoning static, rigid defense architectures, an agile defense plan emphasizes continuous iteration, automation, and cross-functional flexibility. Defensive agility allows cybersecurity teams to rapidly adapt and respond to evolving threats while minimizing business disruption, says Anant Adya, an executive vice president at business and technology consulting firm Infosys. “As attack surfaces expand, organizations must prioritize risk quantification and identify vulnerabilities to strengthen their security posture and improve their ability to recover from attacks that are inevitable.” Is your organization taking the steps needed to achieve a high degree of defensive agility? Read on to find out. 1. Establish a zero-trust baseline Achieving defensive agility should begin with a zero-trust approach that continuously verifies access across users, devices, and applications, Adya advises. “An effective zero-trust strategy must be embedded into an organization’s technology framework and business lifecycle in order to build resilience and foster an organization-wide security mindset.” As enterprises adopt AI, modernize applications, and operate across highly distributed environments, security must evolve from a protective afterthought into a business accelerant, Adya says. “By integrating zero trust into day-to-day operations and AI workflows, organizations can strengthen their ability to adapt to evolving threats while innovating faster, integrating acquisitions more securely, and scaling globally without accumulating architectural or operational debt.” 2. Modernize (and rationalize) your existing security infrastructure Many large organizations are struggling to keep pace with emerging challenges because their systems are incredibly complex or filled with old software, custom code, and a mixture of disconnected security tools that can hinder containment speed, says Sharon Chand, cyber defense and resilience leader at Deloitte. Chand advises CISOs to evaluate their existing infrastructure and technologies to consider how they’re currently responding to threats. Meanwhile, it’s important to streamline operations into a more integrated system. “Security organizations must also have access to AI-driven systems to detect and automate response to machine-speed attacks at the pace of adversaries,” she states. 3. Enlist AI where confidence is high and actions are reversible Randy Gross, CISO at training and certification organization CompTIA, recommends deciding in advance which defensive actions are safe enough to happen without placing a human in the middle. “Locking an account, killing a session, or isolating a device should already be automated when confidence is high and the action is easy to reverse,” he says. Review your strategy at least quarterly, but never equate a strategy review with operational governance, Gross warns. “In a medium-to-large enterprise, agents’ permissions and integrations may change frequently, so the guardrails around them must be continuous and automated,” he advises. “The CISO and team should also revisit their strategy when enough changes have been made to the point where risk has changed materially.” Gross adds: “The strategy shouldn’t be just to put more AI in the SOC; it should be to reduce the latency between finding a threat and doing something useful about it.” 4. Forego higher walls in favor of dynamic, structural resilience Defensive agility requires an enterprise system with the architectural capacity to absorb, isolate, and adapt to anomalous behavior without relying on human intervention, says Jatin Chopra, a senior software engineer at Microsoft. “It marks the transition from static perimeter defense — where you build higher walls — to dynamic, structural resilience where the environment itself constantly shifts to restrict threat propagation.” Using an approach with sufficient capacity also detaches security from manual bottlenecking, Chopra says. “When defensive protocols are codified into the architecture rather than enforced by a review board, engineering teams can maintain high developer velocity while inherently restricting the attack surface.” It transforms security from a workflow tax into an automated platform capability, he states. 5. Beware bureaucracy that does not lead to decisive action Stop treating your security strategy as an annual document process and begin viewing it as a loop that runs continuously utilizing data you trust, says Bob Maley, CISO at security-as-a-service provider Black Kite. Feed decisions to someone who actually has the authority to make rapid critical choices, he recommends. Attackers are already highly vigilant, Maley warns. “When a new vulnerability opportunity lands on a Friday afternoon, nobody on a ransomware crew is waiting for a quarterly review to approve going after it,” he explains. “If your defense team needs a steering committee before it can react, the gap between their tempo and yours is where the breach lives.” 6. Embrace automation to free up human judgment Most security teams I’ve worked with build static defenses, observes Timur Rakhmatullin, senior software engineer at Softline Solutions, a consulting and social media marketing services provider. “They set up rules, configure alerts, and write runbooks, but then something happens that doesn’t match the runbook and everyone freezes.” Rakhmatullin believes that automation is essential. He runs automated security scans across 30-plus repositories using in-house tools. “The scans catch vulnerabilities, license issues, and other gaps,” Rakhmatullin explains. “But the key part is that any engineer can override a scan result, escalate it, or reclassify a finding in minutes.” Still, automation does all the heavy lifting, Rakhmatullin says. “Humans make the judgment calls.” 7. Conduct regular ‘fire drills’ Rehearse ugly scenarios before they happen, suggests Chris McGlasson, founder of ClearStack Advisory, a fractional executive technology and AI strategy firm. Know who patches, who tests, who talks to the business, and who has the authority to take something offline at 2 a.m., McGlasson says. “Write it down and run it twice a year,” he recommends. “The teams that do so treat incident response like a fire drill.” McGlasson adds that many CISOs risk disaster because they treat security like a research project instead of a fundamental initiative. McGlasson points to the recent “Citrix meltdown,” a severe, ongoing security crisis affecting Citrix NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway appliances, creating a mass wave of critical zero-day exploits . Citrix immediately warned IT administrators to patch their systems at once to address the issue. As a result, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, gave federal agencies a three-day patch window, while other organizations were left to create their own timeline, McGlasson says. He notes that the shops that handled this challenging event well weren’t always the ones with the best tools. “They were the ones that already knew who patches, who tests, and who calls the shots before the advisory ever dropped.” Agility is a muscle, McGlasson observes. “You build it through repetition.”

title: Civil servants hit by Capita pension failure may take lead from teachers’ union compensation victory
raw_text:
The government will face a large compensation bill related to failures in the Capita-run Civil Service Pension Scheme (CSPS) administration if members follow the example of teachers who won rights to compensation in the High Court.

The NASUWT Teachers Union announced last week it had secured around £750,000 in financial compensation from the Department for Education for 83 members impacted by failures in the Teachers’ Pension Scheme administration, which was run by Capita for about 20 years up until this month.

Thousands of retired and serving civil servants have been impacted by Capita’s CSPS failures, with many suffering severe financial distress. A campaign group set up to support them said: “We hope the unions will explore the possibility of similar legal action as that taken by teachers, whilst being careful not to raise false hopes.”

The members of the teachers’ pension administration scheme run by Capita have been forced to wait months, and in some cases more than a year, for legally required pension valuations known as cash equivalent transfer values.

The scheme has now switched to Tata Consultancy Services after the migration of accounts late last month and at the beginning of this month.

Matt Wrack, general secretary at NASUWT, said: “We gave the Department for Education (DfE) ample time and opportunity to resolve this matter, but their failure to address this satisfactorily left us with no choice but to take legal action.

“They were left feeling distressed and suffered financial harm because the DfE failed to meet its legal duties,” he added. “Teachers who had paid into their pensions in good faith had every right to expect the [pension scheme] to be there for them when they needed it.”

Computer Weekly asked the Department for Education what responsibility Capita has for the failures and the financial redress, which is now owed as a consequence, but it had not responded when this article was published.

Civil servants watch

Ryan Bradshaw, partner at law firm Leigh Day, which represented the claimants, said: “This regrettable situation has once again highlighted the issues of maladministration that arise all too often when public services are outsourced to private providers.”

There could also be a knock-on effect on the CSPS scheme. The scheme, which has 1.7 million members, switched from MYCSP to Capita in December, after a two-year preparation period. Members of the scheme have since been hit by massive delays in receiving pensions (see timeline below).

If there is a large compensation bill, Capita could be made to pay. In a written parliamentary answer on 26 October 2026, responding to John McDonnell MP, Jameson said: “We intend to seek to recover all the government’s delay-related costs, and that Capita bear the costs of their failure, not the taxpayer.”

The matter of compensation for CSPS members affected has also been raised by MPs campaigning for affected constituents.

Last month, MP Euan Stainbank asked Cabinet Office minister Sally Jameson what consideration she has given to a compensation scheme for those who have experienced delays in administration of their civil service pension. She said in a written statement: “Interest will be paid on delayed benefits to avoid financial loss by members.

“In addition, the existing statutory complaints process evaluates claims for financial losses, as well as distress and inconvenience caused, on a case-by-case basis to determine whether compensation is due. This ensures that any retiree who provides evidence of extra costs, such as bank penalties or interest charges caused by the delay, is fairly assessed. All complaints will be handled with reference to Pensions Ombudsman standards.”

The Civil Service Campaigns Group, made up of people affected by the delays, told Computer Weekly: “This is an encouraging development for CSPS members who have suffered as a result of Capita’s failures. Whilst we don’t yet know whether the legal circumstances are comparable, any opportunity to explore financial redress is certainly welcome.

“Thousands of members continue to be affected by this crisis, suffering financial hardship, mounting debt, emotional distress and deteriorating health as a result of Capita’s maladministration of the scheme and the Cabinet Office’s continued failure to hold the contractor properly to account.

“Our immediate priority remains restoring normal service levels and getting pensions paid without further delay. However, members should not be expected to bear the consequences of failures entirely outside their control.”

Computer Weekly contacted the PCS union, which represents civil servants, but it had no comments at this time.

title: Datacentres of the future will be built differently, says Gartner
raw_text:
“The datacentre of the future is not just built differently. It is justified, approved, operated and governed differently.”

That’s according to Henrique Cecci, senior director analyst at Gartner, who made the case ahead of the Gartner IT Symposium/Xpo in Barcelona this week. For CIOs, he said, the strategic implication is clear: “Datacentre decisions made today must be flexible enough to adapt to the world they will still operate in 20 years from now.”

His argument comes as artificial intelligence (AI) providers prepare to spend nearly $1tn on AI infrastructure in 2026, with a further $6tn forecast between 2027 and 2030, according to Gartner figures. The pressure is evident in datacentres, where Gartner said power density is set to rise 10 times.

“We used to have five, six, seven, eight kilowatts per cabinet. And today we have more than 10, 12 or more kilowatts. Eventually, we’ll have 250 kilowatts per cabinet and more,” Cecci said.

He set out three priorities for CIOs. The first is workload placement – matching each workload to the datacentre that suits it. “At startup, cloud makes total sense, but a large enterprise with all the legacy may be a different mix,” he said.

The second is to secure capacity and energy commitments early. “We have to plan and get commitments in advance because we may not have enough resources eventually,” he said. Colocation vacancy rates are very low, he added, and costs will tend to increase in the coming years.

The third is regulation and sovereignty. “We have increasing regulatory requirements, in terms of energy, water, noise, heat, use and many other things in sustainability,” he said. “We need to have those numbers to show. Sovereignty is a growing trend also.”

Gartner groups the pressures reshaping the datacentre into four forces:

  1. Market economics
  2. Power and technology
  3. Regulation and social licence
  4. Geopolitics and sovereignty

Its research says $130bn of projects were blocked or delayed in the first quarter of 2026, and that datacentre electricity demand will climb toward 1,218TWh (terawatt-hours) by 2030. Its strategic planning assumption holds that, through mid-2027, hardware costs for general-purpose datacentre servers will run 50% to 125% above mid-2025 levels.

Cecci said the response should be datacentres that are more power-aware, redesigned for mixed-density and liquid-cooled zones, distributed by sovereignty and community acceptance, modular and approval-ready. He pointed to modern datacentre infrastructure management (DCIM) tools and digital twins that let operators model what-if scenarios and predict anomalies. The upshot is that power availability, not network connectivity, now decides where a facility goes.

Geopolitics runs through the analysis. Gartner has said 60% of organisations expect geopolitical factors to increase future use of cloud, and that sovereignty concerns are pushing some towards non-US-owned facilities or their own builds.

Cecci said that despite the hyperscale buildout, on-premises datacentres are still viable. “We don’t have one size fits all,” he said. “A strategically located on-premises facility still makes sense for governments, large banks and large organisations that want to keep part of their processing in-house, for sovereignty and low-latency reasons.”

Edge is the other counterweight to the hyperscale buildout. Inference is growing “more than four or five times more than training”, Cecci said, and modular, prefabricated options are reducing the cost of distributed capacity.

The message lands amid a reshaping of planning and power in the UK. The government published the first draft National Policy Statement for datacentres in October – the committed UK datacentre pipeline has grown to more than 14GW, and ministers want at least 6GW of AI-capable capacity by 2030. Grid connection reform and a pause on large Scottish planning decisions complete the picture.

title: Google Cloud London outage: Continuity lessons for IT leaders
raw_text:
On 20 October, a power event at the datacentre hosting Google Cloud’s europe-west2-b zone took that zone offline. It is one of three availability zones in Google’s London region, designed to allow the others to keep running if one experiences a fault. Yet Revolut, HSBC, DPD and Royal Mail were among the organisations reported to have experienced disruption, and critically, the video platform used for remote court hearings in England and Wales also went down. 

Google’s preliminary incident report found that the failure caused secondary failover and queuing delays across infrastructure that had not lost power. Google has said it will publish a final report with preventative actions. The engineering findings will be worth reading. 

For IT leaders, the most important lesson isn’t that a major cloud provider experienced an outage. It’s that infrastructure resilience and business resilience are not necessarily the same thing. The real test is whether an organisation can maintain or recover its critical services when the infrastructure it depends on becomes unavailable. 

A simple place to start is to pick a single zone that hosts part of their estate, work out what would stop working if it went offline, and estimate how long recovery would take. 

Find dependencies nobody has mapped

A zone can be well isolated while an application that runs across several zones still depends on just one of them. Applications are built from many parts, including databases, message queues, identity services, DNS and third-party software – if one of them sits in a single zone, the whole service may be exposed to an outage there. 

The same applies to suppliers. A payment provider or software-as-a-service tool may run in the affected zone while your own infrastructure sits elsewhere, but your customers will still feel the impact. 

One practical way to start is to choose the one service the business could least afford to lose and follow a customer journey through it, from the first click to the final confirmation. For every component along the way, write down which region and zone it runs in and what it depends on in turn, then ask each supplier involved the same question.

What “if feasible” means in practice

During the incident, Google’s advice to affected customers was to migrate impacted workloads to another available location, “if feasible”. Whether that is possible very much depends on decisions made before an outage starts. 

The first is authority. Someone needs to be named as able to trigger a failover, and they need to know it. The second is cost – standby capacity and replicated data both appear on the bill, so the decision to move needs a budget holder who has agreed to it in advance. Finally, there is rehearsal. A plan that has never been tested is likely to contain assumptions that only come up under pressure. 

A rehearsal can be simple – a scheduled exercise in working hours with someone keeping time and someone taking notes will show how long recovery really takes and where roles or instructions are unclear. 

Matching protection to business impact

Not every workload warrants the same level of protection, and paying for the highest tier everywhere is rarely practical for a mid-sized organisation. IT leaders need to make sure they weigh costs of protection against the consequences of downtime. 

For each service, ask what happens if it is unavailable for an hour, for four hours and for a day, in terms of revenue, customers, regulatory obligations and staff. The answers set two targets – how long the service can be down, and how much recent data can be lost (commonly called the recovery time and recovery point objectives). 

Services will often fall into three groups. Those that the business cannot do without justify running across multiple zones, with a failover that has been tested. The middle group can usually be restored from backups into another zone or region within an agreed time. The remainder can be rebuilt from code and backups, and an outage of several hours is acceptable for them. 

Resilience shouldn’t be measured by how much an organisation spends on redundancy, but by whether that investment reflects the commercial impact of downtime. Protecting every workload to the highest possible standard is rarely practical or financially justified. The objective should be to invest proportionately to ensure the services most critical to revenue, customers and operations receive the greatest protection.

Cloud resilience operates on a shared-responsibility model. While providers are accountable for the infrastructure and services they deliver, organisations remain responsible for understanding how their applications are architected, where dependencies exist and whether recovery strategies meet business requirements. The big AWS outage in the US in October 2025 was a reminder that disruption can extend beyond the infrastructure where a fault begins. 

Agree recovery responsibilities with cloud and support partners

Most critical services depend on several parties, whether a hyperscale provider, a managed service provider, a software vendor or an internal platform team. During an incident, delays often come from uncertainty over who is responsible for each step. It helps to record that division of responsibility for every critical workload in a straightforward format. At a minimum, it should show where the workload runs, which services it relies on, who has failover authority, and committed response times for each party. 

Technology partners should play a proactive role in this process. Beyond responding to incidents, they should help customers challenge assumptions about their environments, identify single points of failure and assess whether the cost of additional resilience is justified by the business risk it mitigates. A partner supporting the environment should be able to produce that evidence, along with a costed view of moving a given service to a higher tier of protection. This gives IT leaders a clearer picture of the protection they have, gaps that remain and the cost to address them. 

Settling decisions before the next incident

Power faults, software changes and human error can interrupt cloud services on any provider, and the Google Cloud incident shows how far the effects can travel beyond the zone where a fault begins. No business can prevent every outage, but can look at how much disruption its business can tolerate and prepare accordingly. Leaders need to be clear about which services matter most, what level of recovery each one requires and who is accountable for acting when a provider’s status page starts to change. 

Those decisions need to be revisited as the business and its systems change. A team that has agreed costs, assigned responsibility and rehearsed its recovery steps is better placed to respond when the next incident occurs than one trying to work out what to do under pressure. 

The next major cloud outage is a question of when, not if. The organisations that navigate it most effectively won’t necessarily be those spending the most on infrastructure, but those that understand their dependencies, have made informed investment decisions and have tested their ability to recover. For technology leaders, the question is simple: if a critical cloud service failed tomorrow, could you demonstrate that your business is ready?

title: AC/DC: The AI power reckoning driving a shift to high-density DC
raw_text:
Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping the datacentre landscape at extraordinary speed. Hyperscale operators are racing to deploy infrastructure capable of supporting increasingly power-hungry workloads, with more than 100GW of new AI datacentre capacity expected worldwide between 2026 and 2030.

At the heart of this shift is a fundamental change in compute density. Traditional server racks typically operate at around 10kW. Today, AI racks are approaching 1MW, which represents a two orders of magnitude increase in power demand within the same physical footprint. This escalation is set to expose a critical constraint that has, until now, remained largely invisible. Namely, the limitations of the underlying energy architecture in sustaining future demand.

The limitations of AC infrastructure

Despite the digital nature of modern computing, the energy systems that power datacentres remain rooted in a model developed more than a century ago. Alternating current (AC) became the standard because it enabled efficient long-distance transmission at a time when direct current (DC) could not.

However, every core component inside a datacentre, from GPUs to batteries, fundamentally operates on DC power. As a result, today’s infrastructure relies on a continuous cycle of conversions. 

AC from the grid is stepped down, converted to DC for storage, inverted back to AC for distribution, and finally converted again to DC at the chip level. This process introduces a “conversion tax” – between 10% and 30% of incoming energy can be lost before it ever reaches the compute load. 

These losses create a double penalty – this valuable energy is lost as heat, which means this heat must then be removed using cooling systems and this requires additional energy consumption.

In an era where power availability is becoming a limiting factor for datacentre expansion, every percentage point of efficiency matters. Each incremental loss represents not only reduced compute capacity from a fixed grid connection, but also substantial financial impact at scale. Across gigawatt-class facilities, even a single percentage point of inefficiency can translate into millions in lost value and reinforces the need to maximise the proportion of energy that reaches the processors themselves.

Why AI forces a move to DC

Historically, these inefficiencies were tolerable. Rack densities were low enough that energy losses could be absorbed without fundamentally constraining performance. AI changes this.

With racks that approach megawatt scale, the physical and thermal limits of AC infrastructure are being reached. NVIDIA and other technology leaders now advocate for 800VDC architectures as the only viable path to support megawatt-scale racks.

The rationale is straightforward. Higher voltage DC systems enable lower current for the same power delivery, reduce resistive losses and allow significantly more power to be transmitted through existing conductors. In practical terms, 800VDC can deliver substantially more power while reducing copper usage, installation complexity and cost. But, to implement this requires a fundamental redesign of how energy is delivered within the datacentre.

Mapping the transition from AC To DC

The transition to DC-native architecture is not a single step, but a staged evolution. Today, most datacentres operate in what we can call Stage 0, where power is distributed entirely in AC, with DC conversion at the point of use.

Stage 1 would introduce targeted improvements through retrofits such as sidecar solutions that enable the introduction of 800VDC racks, and result in 85% to 93% system efficiency. While valuable, these approaches are widely viewed as interim measures.

A more significant shift occurs with Stage 2, where elements of the infrastructure – mainly the UPS systems – begin to operate on DC. This hybrid approach removes unnecessary conversions, so system efficiency can increase to 91% to 96%.

The real shift begins at Stage 3, where datacentres become fundamentally DC-native. Here, traditional transformers are replaced by solid-state transformers that convert medium voltage AC directly to DC. This simplifies the power chain and unlocks efficiency of 94% to 97%.

Stage 4 builds on this with fully integrated DC architecture that combines advanced ultra-efficient solid state transformers connected directly to 34.5kV grids, DC-based UPS systems, and intelligent energy management. At this stage, total system efficiencies approach 98%, dramatically increasing the proportion of incoming power that can be used for compute.

While some operators will progress incrementally, leapfrogging intermediate stages entirely is ultimately more cost-effective and optimises operations. For datacentres planned today, designing for 800V DC rather than preparing to retrofit this architecture will likely prove the more effective approach.

Solid state transformers: The Holy Grail of DC architecture

At the core of this transition is the solid-state transformer (SST). Unlike conventional transformers, which are typically large, site-specific and limited in functionality, solid-state transformers will integrate conversion and control into a single, modular system. They are designed to connect directly to medium-voltage grid infrastructure and deliver high-voltage DC in a single step and eliminate multiple layers of conversion. Advancements in semiconductor materials, particularly silicon carbide, are enabling SSTs to operate at higher voltages with lower switching losses, and improve efficiency and performance.

Beyond efficiency gains, solid-state transformers can offer additional advantages. Their modular design allows for faster manufacturing and deployment compared to traditional bespoke transformers, reducing lead times and enabling quicker time to operation. Built-in redundancy at the module level also enhances system resilience while ensuring no single point of failure.

But, technical challenges remain. Although 800VDC architecture already exists in utility scale solar and electric vehicles, implementing it for SSTs is no easy feat. Directly interfacing with grid-level voltages, such as Europe’s 33kV grid or the 34.5KV grid in the US, without intermediate conversion stages is complex and requires much expertise in DC energy architecture. 

Implications for the grid

The benefits of DC architecture extend beyond the datacentre itself. As power demand from AI infrastructure grows, concerns around grid capacity and stability intensify. In many regions, access to sufficient power is already limiting datacentre expansion. By improving energy efficiency, DC-native systems enable operators to extract more compute from the same grid connection and reduce the need for additional capacity. Lower losses also translate into reduced cooling requirements, further easing overall energy demand.

In addition, integrating DC-based energy storage and intelligent control systems should allow datacentres to interact with the grid more dynamically. DC UPS systems, for example, can act as a buffer to smooth demand fluctuations and mitigate the impact of sudden load changes.

Overcoming barriers to adoption

Despite the clear benefits, the transition to DC is not without challenges. First, there is the question of infrastructure change. Moving beyond early-stage retrofits requires replacing key components within the power chain, which can be complex.

Second, regulatory frameworks for DC systems are not yet fully mature. Standards for safety, certification, and operation are still being developed, particularly for higher voltage levels. Finally, there is a skills gap – designing and deploying DC-native systems requires specialist expertise that is not yet widespread across the industry. However, these challenges are typical of any major technological shift and with the groundwork already being laid, solutions will soon appear.

The transition timeline

This transition is already taking shape. 2026 is expected to see a few prototyping and early pilot deployments of DC architectures and solid-state transformers. By 2027, SSTs are expected to be commercially available and initial commercial projects should emerge. From 2028 onwards, as megawatt-scale AI racks become mainstream, DC infrastructure will need to scale rapidly to meet demand. 

Looking further ahead, the industry is already considering a future transition to 1500VDC systems. While this offers additional efficiency gains, it introduces new technical and safety challenges that will need to be addressed through further innovation and standardisation.

The inevitability of evolution

As AI continues to push the boundaries of power density, the limitations of traditional infrastructure are being reached. DC architecture offers a path to higher efficiency, greater scalability and improved alignment with the needs of next-generation workloads.

The question is no longer whether this transition will happen, but how quickly the industry can execute it. Datacentres are the first to face this challenge at scale, but they are unlikely to be the last. As the technology matures, the shift towards DC-native energy systems may prove to be far more widespread.

title: Gartner Symposium: Keeping the tech flywheel under control
raw_text:
Analyst firm Gartner opened its annual symposium in Barcelona with images of a drift car, depicting the challenges organisations face in driving forward a technology strategy when external forces appear to be uncontrollable.

Its message to CIO and IT leadership delegates was that as they shape outcomes, today’s breakthroughs quickly become tomorrow’s expectations. Discussing the metaphor, Gartner chief fellow Daryl Plummer said: “In drift car racing, you shift your momentum through braking. Managing the drag to shape the agenda. This is what it feels like in AI [artificial intelligence] – we are all in full opposite lock.”

In the opening keynote, Plummer warned: “Last year on this stage, we said only one in five AI projects succeed. Well, this year, it’s still one in five. However, 58% of executives now tell us that they get positive ROI [return on investment] from AI. That means that the one project that succeeds drives the bulk of ROI value gained.”

He said IT departments are now spending 18 times more than they did two years ago to achieve a return on their AI investment, adding: “It matters now more than ever that you pick the right AI projects.”

Gartner sees the greatest value AI can add to an organisation as creating work that was not possible before. But this does not mean deploying AI tools across the business. As Computer Weekly has previously reported, doing so without careful monitoring of usage can lead to unbudgeted costs.

Beyond the economic impact, there are risks from employees Gartner dubs “hero innovators”. People want to use AI to achieve business outcomes, but in doing so, they introduce cyber security risks. They usually understand not to share sensitive internal data, but may inadvertently do so when trying to use agentic AI to achieve a task. “Agentic AI is worse than heroin; it’s addictive and causes you to do things you may not otherwise want to do,” Plummer warned. 

He said CIOs are living in a risk-dominant world. Gartner research has found that 86% of CIOs see risk growing faster than value, but the value potential is very high. “Your need to build AI value is strong, but your ability to govern the risk is weak,” he said. “As a CIO, the best thing you can do is to align value with risk.”

Looking at the rise in AI threats, distinguished vice-president and Gartner fellow Kristin Moyer said: “In 10 years, AI could take your company to a trillion-dollar valuation, but it may do enormous damage to your business much sooner. You live between these extremes.”

While CIOs strive to build positive value with AI, and to do so safely, Moyer said they need to battle against external bad actors and internal AI innovators who work against AI safety.

The keynote covered a range of topics relating to risk and sovereign capabilities. The analyst firm depicts risk and value as two flywheels connected through a governance model. Among the recommendations from Gartner for addressing an over-reliance on non-homegrown tech is to use optionality in AI decision-making and develop independence through contractual agreement.

One area of risk IT leaders should consider seriously is the advent of quantum computing, which will be powerful enough to crack modern encryption. In the European Union, member states have a coordinated roadmap to transition high-risk use cases to post-quantum cryptography (PQC) by 2030.

Plummer warned that in certain organisations like government departments, records may be over 50 years old and need to be held for 50 years into the future. He warned that the risk is not that the data can be stolen – as data loss is something that organisations do experience – but that the stolen data can be decrypted unless it is protected by PQC.

title: Energy giant signs contract for foundational digital services
raw_text:
Energy supplier SSE Group has signed a deal with Atos for IT services that will underpin its £33bn transformation programme.

Atos is to provide the digital foundations for the project, which will see SSE, formerly known as Scottish and Southern Energy, invest billions in electricity networks and renewables.

The five-year contract also includes Atos supplying computing services to SSE’s 14,000 staff.

Announced a year ago, SSE Group said the £33bn investment plan would “help build a cleaner, more secure and more affordable energy system”.

SSE CIO Stewart Fry said the company needed a supplier to help put in place the digital foundations for the project. “As we focus on our programme to transform the UK’s electricity infrastructure and deliver long-term benefits for society, we need foundational digital services we can rely on, that are intelligent, secure and future-ready.”

Atos has a significant customer base in the energy sector, including EDF and the National Grid, where it works on a project known as Triton, a digital twin and data visualisation tool that replaced highly manual, labour-intensive and time-consuming electricity network modelling.

“We needed a partner who understood the complex needs of a business like ours, delivering vital always-on services to our customers,” added Fry.

Atos’s contract covers service integration and management services, digital workplace, cloud operations and data management.

The computing services for SSE staff will provide proactive monitoring, so problems are fixed before employees are affected, Atos said. “Device life will be extended through proactive maintenance, performance-based refreshes and remanufactured devices, which supports SSE’s environmental goals,” it added.

SSE will also have access to Atos’s centre of excellence for critical national infrastructure, which provides services to sectors such as energy, rail, water and aerospace. According to Atos, the centre is “designed to tackle complex industry challenges through collaboration and knowledge sharing across the sector and its regulators”.

Michael Herron, head of Atos in the UK, said: “We understand that the service SSE provides is critical and resilience is essential and will work to strengthen its infrastructure, support the people who keep it running and protect essential services with mission-critical experience, sovereign security and next-generation technology.”

Wider Atos strategy

Atos is also investing in education for young people. It has recently made several commitments to educating the UK’s youth.

In February, also in the West Midlands, Atos’s first UK apprentices began training to become IT staff of the future as part of a programme to support professionals in the era of AI. Atos’s agentic factory, which will feature AI agents and people working together on customer IT projects, was opened at the supplier’s delivery centre in Solihull, on the outskirts of Birmingham.

Also in the West Midlands, Atos recently said it was investing money into Tech First Youth’s Future Readiness initiative, which will see schools and colleges in the region receive free access to resources. It will have a focus on AI discernment, which is the ability to identify when AI outputs should be used or when caution is required.

Although AI is a concept dating back decades, the widespread take-up of generative AI began around 2022, with the release of ChatGPT.
